title: Revisiting maternal and child undernutrition in low-income and middle-income countries: variable progress towards an unfinished agenda
abstract: 13 years after the first Lancet Series on maternal and child undernutrition, we reviewed the progress achieved on the basis of global estimates and new analyses of 50 low-income and middle-income countries with national surveys from around 2000 and 2015. The prevalence of childhood stunting has fallen, and linear growth faltering in early life has become less pronounced over time, markedly in middle-income countries but less so in low-income countries. Stunting and wasting remain public health problems in low-income countries, where 4·7% of children are simultaneously affected by both, a condition associated with a 4·8-times increase in mortality.
summary:
The paper "Revisiting maternal and child undernutrition in low-income and middle-income countries: variable progress towards an unfinished agenda" by Victora et al. aims to assess progress in addressing maternal and child undernutrition in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) since the first Lancet Series on this topic. The authors conducted a comprehensive review of global estimates and analyzed data from national surveys in 50 LMICs from 2000 and 2015.

Key findings indicate a decline in childhood stunting, particularly in middle-income countries, while low-income countries continue to face significant challenges, with 4.7% of children affected by both stunting and wasting, which is linked to a 4.8-fold increase in mortality risk. The prevalence of low birthweight has decreased slowly, and new evidence suggests that undernutrition may begin at birth. Additionally, high rates of micronutrient deficiencies persist, particularly in Africa and South Asia.

The authors conclude that despite some progress, maternal and child undernutrition remains a critical global health issue, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. They emphasize the need for multisectoral interventions addressing the social determinants of undernutrition, including poverty and education, to accelerate progress towards global nutrition targets. The paper highlights the importance of early-life nutrition and calls for improved data collection on maternal and child health indicators to inform effective policy and intervention strategies.

filename: Interaction between microbiota and immunity in health and disease.pdf
title: Interaction between microbiota and immunity in health and disease
abstract: The interplay between the commensal microbiota and the mammalian immune system development and function includes multifold interactions in homeostasis and disease. The microbiome plays critical roles in the training and development of major components of the host’s innate and adaptive immune system, while the immune system orchestrates the maintenance of key features of host-microbe symbiosis. In a genetically susceptible host, imbalances in microbiota-immunity interactions under defined environmental contexts are believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of a multitude of immune-mediated disorders. Here, we review features of microbiome-immunity crosstalk and their roles in health and disease, while providing examples of molecular mechanisms orchestrating these interactions in the intestine and extra-intestinal organs.
summary:
The review article by Zheng et al. explores the complex interactions between the microbiota and the immune system, emphasizing their roles in health and disease. The main objective is to elucidate how microbiome-immunity crosstalk influences immune system development and function, and how imbalances in these interactions can lead to immune-mediated disorders.

The authors employ a comprehensive literature review, synthesizing findings from various studies that utilize germ-free animal models and human observations to illustrate the mechanisms of microbiota-immune interactions. They highlight the significance of early-life microbial colonization in shaping immune responses and the bidirectional communication between microbiota and both innate and adaptive immune systems.

Key findings indicate that the microbiome is crucial for the maturation of immune cells, the maintenance of immune tolerance, and the prevention of inflammatory diseases. Disruptions in microbiota composition, often due to environmental factors like diet and antibiotic use, are linked to conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), allergies, and autoimmune disorders. The review also discusses specific microbial metabolites and immune signaling pathways that mediate these interactions.

In conclusion, the authors stress the need for further research to clarify the causal relationships between microbiome dysbiosis and immune dysfunction. Understanding these interactions could lead to innovative microbiome-targeted therapies for various immune-mediated diseases, highlighting the potential for personalized medicine approaches in treating such conditions.

title: A Diet Enriched with the Omega-3 Fatty Acid Docosahexaenoic Acid Reduces Amyloid Burden in an Aged Alzheimer Mouse Model
abstract: Epidemiological studies suggest that increased intake of the omega-3 (n-3) polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is associated with reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). DHA levels are lower in serum and brains of AD patients, which could result from low dietary intake and/or PUFA oxidation. Because effects of DHA on Alzheimer pathogenesis, particularly on amyloidosis, are unknown, we used the APPsw (Tg2576) transgenic mouse model to evaluate the impact of dietary DHA on amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing and amyloid burden. Aged animals (17–19 months old) were placed in one of three groups until 22.5 months of age: control (0.09% DHA), low-DHA (0%), or high-DHA (0.6%) chow. α-Amyloid (Aβ) ELISA of the detergent-insoluble extract of cortical homogenates showed that DHA-enriched diets significantly reduced total Aβ by ~70% when compared with low-DHA or control chow diets. Dietary DHA also decreased Aβ42 levels below those seen with control chow. Image analysis of brain sections with an antibody against Aβ revealed that overall plaque burden was significantly reduced by 40.3%, with the largest reductions (40–50%) in the hippocampus and parietal cortex. DHA modulated APP processing by decreasing both β- and α-APP C-terminal fragment products and full-length APP. BACE1 (β-secretase activity of the β-site APP-cleaving enzyme), ApoE (apolipoprotein E), and transthyretin gene expression were unchanged with the high-DHA diet. Together, these results suggest that dietary DHA could be protective against Aβ production, accumulation, and potential downstream toxicity.
summary:
The main objective of this study was to investigate the effects of dietary docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid, on amyloid burden and amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing in an aged transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). 

To achieve this, aged Tg2576 mice were divided into three dietary groups: control (0.09% DHA), low-DHA (0%), and high-DHA (0.6%). The researchers measured levels of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides and assessed plaque burden using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) and immunohistochemistry.

Key findings revealed that a high-DHA diet significantly reduced total insoluble Aβ levels by approximately 70% and plaque burden by about 40%, particularly in vulnerable brain regions like the hippocampus and parietal cortex. The high-DHA diet also decreased levels of Aβ42, while APP processing was modulated, resulting in lower levels of both amyloidogenic and non-amyloidogenic APP fragments. Notably, the expression of BACE1 (the enzyme responsible for Aβ production) remained unchanged, suggesting that DHA's effects were not due to alterations in secretase expression but rather influenced APP processing pathways.

In conclusion, the study suggests that dietary DHA may offer protective effects against amyloid production and accumulation in the context of AD. These findings support the potential of DHA as a dietary intervention to reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease, particularly in older populations, highlighting its role in modulating neurodegenerative processes.

title: Gut microbiome alterations in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia. However, the etiopathogenesis of this devastating disease is not fully understood. Recent studies in rodents suggest that alterations in the gut microbiome may contribute to amyloid deposition, yet the microbial communities associated with AD have not been characterized in humans. Towards this end, we characterized the bacterial taxonomic composition of fecal samples from participants with and without a diagnosis of dementia due to AD. Our analyses revealed that the gut microbiome of AD participants has decreased microbial diversity and is compositionally distinct from control age- and sex-matched individuals. We identified phylum- through genus-wide differences in bacterial abundance including decreased Firmicutes, increased Bacteroidetes, and decreased Bifidobacterium in the microbiome of AD participants. Furthermore, we observed correlations between levels of differentially abundant genera and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers of AD. These findings add AD to the growing list of diseases associated with gut microbial alterations, as well as suggest that gut bacterial communities may be a target for therapeutic intervention.
summary:
The main objective of the study was to investigate alterations in the gut microbiome of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) compared to age- and sex-matched controls, and to explore the relationship between these microbiome changes and AD pathology as indicated by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers.

To achieve this, the researchers conducted bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing on fecal samples from 25 participants with AD and 25 controls. They analyzed the microbial composition, richness, and diversity, and correlated the findings with CSF biomarkers related to AD pathology, including amyloid-β and phosphorylated tau levels.

Key findings revealed that the gut microbiome of AD participants exhibited significantly decreased microbial diversity and richness, with notable taxonomic differences. Specifically, there was a decrease in Firmicutes and Bifidobacterium, and an increase in Bacteroidetes in the AD group. Moreover, certain genera showed correlations with CSF biomarkers, where increased abundance of specific bacteria was associated with greater AD pathology.

The study concludes that gut microbiome alterations are associated with Alzheimer’s disease, suggesting a potential link between gut health and neurodegenerative processes. These findings imply that targeting gut microbiota could be a novel therapeutic approach for AD, warranting further investigation into the gut-brain axis and its implications for disease progression and treatment strategies.

title: Role of Vitamin D in the Hygiene Hypothesis: The Interplay between Vitamin D, Vitamin D Receptors, Gut Microbiota, and Immune Response
abstract: The hygiene hypothesis postulates that higher levels of cleanliness and improper exposure to microorganisms early in childhood could disturb the intestinal microbiome resulting in abnormal immune responses. Recently, more attention has been put on how a lack of sun exposure and consequently vitamin D deficiency could lead to less immune tolerance and aberrant immune responses. Moreover, vitamin D receptor (VDR) function has been positioned to be a critical aspect of immune response and gut homeostasis. Therefore, this review focuses on the role that the interaction between vitamin D, VDR function, and gut microbiome might have on autoimmune diseases in the context of the hygiene hypothesis.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Clark and Mach (2016) is to explore the interplay between vitamin D, vitamin D receptors (VDR), gut microbiota, and immune responses within the context of the hygiene hypothesis, particularly regarding the rise of autoimmune diseases in Western societies.

The authors conducted a systematic review of existing literature, analyzing studies related to the hygiene hypothesis, gut microbiota, vitamin D, VDR functions, and autoimmune diseases. They included various types of studies, such as randomized controlled trials and observational studies, focusing on the relationship between vitamin D deficiency, VDR dysfunction, and changes in gut microbiota composition.

Key findings indicate a strong correlation between vitamin D deficiency, VDR dysfunction, and altered gut microbiota, which may contribute to the development of autoimmune diseases. The active form of vitamin D, 1,25(OH)2D3, is crucial for VDR activation, influencing immune responses and maintaining gut homeostasis. The review highlights that a hygienic lifestyle and reduced microbial exposure can lead to decreased gut microbiota diversity, resulting in heightened immune responses and increased susceptibility to autoimmune conditions.

In conclusion, the authors suggest that the rising rates of autoimmune diseases in Western countries may be linked to vitamin D deficiency, VDR dysfunction, and a lack of gut microbiota diversity. They emphasize the importance of understanding the interactions between vitamin D, VDRs, and gut microbiota to develop strategies for preventing autoimmune diseases. This research underscores the need for increased awareness of vitamin D's role in immune regulation and gut health, particularly in the context of modern lifestyle changes.

title: Alterations of the human gut microbiome in multiple sclerosis
abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in immune function and has been implicated in several autoimmune disorders. Here we use 16S rRNA sequencing to investigate the gut microbiome in subjects with multiple sclerosis (MS, n = 60) and healthy controls (n = 43). Microbiome alterations in MS include increases in Methanobrevibacter and Akkermansia and decreases in Butyricimonas, and correlate with variations in the expression of genes involved in dendritic cell maturation, interferon signalling and NF-kB signalling pathways in circulating T cells and monocytes. Patients on disease-modifying treatment show increased abundances of Prevotella and Sutterella, and decreased Sarcina, compared with untreated patients. MS patients of a second cohort show elevated breath methane compared with controls, consistent with our observation of increased gut Methanobrevibacter in MS in the first cohort. Further study is required to assess whether the observed alterations in the gut microbiome play a role in, or are a consequence of, MS pathogenesis.
summary:
The main objective of the study was to investigate alterations in the gut microbiome of individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS) compared to healthy controls and to assess the potential correlation between these microbiome changes and immune responses associated with the disease. 

The researchers employed 16S rRNA sequencing to analyze fecal samples from 60 MS patients and 43 healthy controls. They utilized two sequencing platforms (Roche 454 and Illumina MiSeq) to ensure comprehensive data collection and minimize platform-specific biases. The study also included gene expression profiling and breath methane measurements to explore the relationship between microbiome composition and immune function.

Key findings revealed that MS patients exhibited increased levels of Methanobrevibacter and Akkermansia, alongside decreased levels of Butyricimonas, compared to healthy controls. These microbiome alterations correlated with variations in immune gene expression related to dendritic cell maturation and inflammatory signaling pathways. Additionally, patients undergoing disease-modifying treatments showed increased abundances of Prevotella and Sutterella, suggesting that treatment may normalize some microbiome changes associated with MS. Notably, elevated breath methane levels were observed in a second cohort of MS patients, consistent with the increased presence of Methanobrevibacter.

In conclusion, the study highlights significant differences in the gut microbiome of MS patients, which may influence immune responses and disease progression. The findings suggest potential avenues for developing new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiome in MS. Further research is warranted to clarify whether these microbiome changes contribute to MS pathogenesis or are a consequence of the disease.

title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
abstract: This review evaluates the effectiveness of omega-3 fatty acids in the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
summary:
The main objective of the systematic review by Abdelhamid et al. (2018) was to evaluate the effectiveness of omega-3 fatty acids in the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD). The review aimed to determine whether omega-3 supplementation could reduce cardiovascular events, mortality, and other related outcomes.

The authors conducted a comprehensive analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared omega-3 fatty acid supplementation with control interventions. They included studies that assessed various outcomes, such as all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and incidence of cardiovascular events. The review synthesized data using meta-analyses to derive pooled estimates of effect.

Key findings indicated that omega-3 fatty acids did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality or cardiovascular mortality in the general population. However, some subgroup analyses suggested potential benefits in specific populations, such as those with existing cardiovascular conditions. The review also highlighted that higher doses of omega-3s might be more effective in reducing cardiovascular events compared to lower doses.

In conclusion, the review found limited evidence supporting the use of omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of CVD. The authors suggested that while omega-3 supplementation may have some benefits, particularly in certain subgroups, it should not be universally recommended for CVD prevention. The implications of this review emphasize the need for personalized approaches to dietary supplementation and further research to clarify the role of omega-3 fatty acids in cardiovascular health.

title: Probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics and insulin sensitivity
abstract: Animal studies indicate that the composition of gut microbiota may be involved in the progression of insulin resistance to type 2 diabetes. Probiotics and/or prebiotics could be a promising approach to improve insulin sensitivity by favourably modifying the composition of the gut microbial community, reducing intestinal endotoxin concentrations and decreasing energy harvest. The aim of the present review was to investigate the effects of probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics (a combination of probiotics and prebiotics) on insulin resistance in human clinical trials and to discuss the potential mechanisms whereby probiotics and prebiotics improve glucose metabolism.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Kim, Keogh, and Clifton is to investigate the effects of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics on insulin resistance in human clinical trials and to explore the mechanisms by which these interventions may improve glucose metabolism.

The authors conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature, searching databases like PubMed and Cochrane for human intervention studies related to probiotics and prebiotics. They analyzed various clinical trials to assess the impact of these dietary interventions on insulin sensitivity and glucose control.

Key findings indicate that probiotics and prebiotics can positively influence insulin sensitivity through several mechanisms, including the reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, improved gut microbiota composition, decreased intestinal permeability, and increased production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. These SCFAs may enhance the secretion of incretin hormones, which regulate insulin and glucagon levels, thereby improving glucose homeostasis. However, the results from human studies are mixed, with some showing significant benefits while others report no effects on glucose control.

The authors conclude that while there is potential for probiotics and prebiotics to serve as dietary therapies for preventing and managing type 2 diabetes, the current evidence is insufficient. They emphasize the need for more well-designed clinical trials to clarify the effects of specific strains, dosages, and treatment durations on insulin resistance. This research could lead to more effective dietary recommendations for diabetes prevention and management.

title: Intermittent fasting combined with calorie restriction is effective for weight loss and cardio-protection in obese women
abstract: This study examined the effects of intermittent fasting (IF) combined with calorie restriction (CR) on body weight, body composition, and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk in obese women. Obese women (n = 54) were randomized to either the IFCR-liquid or IFCR-food based diet. Results showed that body weight decreased more in the IFCR-liquid group compared to the IFCR-food group. The findings suggest that IF combined with CR and liquid meals is an effective strategy to help obese women lose weight and lower CHD risk.
summary:
The study aimed to evaluate the effects of intermittent fasting (IF) combined with calorie restriction (CR) on weight loss and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk factors in obese women. Specifically, it compared the outcomes of a liquid diet (IFCR-L) versus a food-based diet (IFCR-F) over an 8-week weight loss period following a 2-week weight maintenance phase.

Fifty-four obese women were randomized into two groups: IFCR-L and IFCR-F. The weight loss phase involved a calorie-restricted diet with a fasting day each week. Body weight, fat mass, visceral fat, and various CHD risk indicators were measured.

Key findings revealed that the IFCR-L group experienced a greater weight loss (3.9 kg) compared to the IFCR-F group (2.5 kg), with significant reductions in total and LDL cholesterol levels and improvements in LDL particle size observed only in the IFCR-L group. Both diets reduced fat mass and visceral fat, but the IFCR-L group showed superior results in terms of weight loss and lipid profile improvements.

In conclusion, the combination of intermittent fasting with calorie restriction, particularly using liquid meal replacements, is an effective strategy for promoting weight loss and reducing CHD risk factors in obese women. These findings suggest that this dietary approach could be beneficial for long-term health improvements and weight management in this population.

filename: Defining a Healthy Diet_ Evidence for The Role of Contemporary Dietary Patterns .pdf
title: Defining a Healthy Diet: Evidence for the Role of Contemporary Dietary Patterns in Health and Disease
abstract: The definition of what constitutes a healthy diet is continually shifting to reflect the evolving understanding of the roles that different foods, essential nutrients, and other food components play in health and disease. A large and growing body of evidence supports that intake of certain types of nutrients, specific food groups, or overarching dietary patterns positively influences health and promotes the prevention of common non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Greater consumption of health-promoting foods and limited intake of unhealthier options are intrinsic to the eating habits of certain regional diets such as the Mediterranean diet or have been constructed as part of dietary patterns designed to reduce disease risk, such as the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) or Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diets. In comparison with a more traditional Western diet, these healthier alternatives are higher in plant-based foods, including fresh fruits and vegetables, whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts and lower in animal-based foods, particularly fatty and processed meats. To better understand the current concept of a 'healthy diet,' this review describes the features and supporting clinical and epidemiologic data for diets that have been shown to prevent disease and/or positively influence health.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Cena and Calder is to define a healthy diet by examining contemporary dietary patterns and their roles in health and disease prevention, particularly concerning non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like cardiovascular disease and cancer. 

The authors conducted a narrative review, analyzing clinical and epidemiological data from various dietary patterns, including the Mediterranean diet, DASH, and MIND diets, to understand their health impacts. They highlighted the characteristics of these diets, which emphasize high consumption of plant-based foods, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats while limiting processed foods, red meats, and added sugars.

Key findings indicate that adherence to these health-promoting dietary patterns is associated with reduced risks of NCDs. For instance, the Mediterranean diet has been linked to lower cardiovascular risk, while the DASH diet has shown significant blood pressure reductions. The MIND diet, which combines elements of the Mediterranean and DASH diets, is associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes that a healthy diet is characterized by a balance of macronutrients and micronutrients, primarily derived from whole, plant-based foods. The authors suggest that adopting these dietary patterns can significantly improve health outcomes and reduce the burden of NCDs. The implications of this research underscore the importance of public health initiatives promoting these dietary patterns to enhance population health and prevent chronic diseases.

title: The Human Gut Microbiome – A Potential Controller of Wellness and Disease
abstract: Interest toward the human microbiome, particularly gut microbiome has flourished in recent decades owing to the rapidly advancing sequence-based screening and humanized gnotobiotic model in interrogating the dynamic operations of commensal microbiota. Although this field is still at a very preliminary stage, whereby the functional properties of the complex gut microbiome remain less understood, several promising findings have been documented and exhibit great potential toward revolutionizing disease etiology and medical treatments. In this review, the interactions between gut microbiota and the host have been focused on, to provide an overview of the role of gut microbiota and their unique metabolites in conferring host protection against invading pathogen, regulation of diverse host physiological functions including metabolism, development and homeostasis of immunity and the nervous system.
summary:
The paper titled "The Human Gut Microbiome – A Potential Controller of Wellness and Disease" by Kho and Lal aims to explore the complex interactions between the human gut microbiome and host health, emphasizing its role in disease etiology and potential therapeutic applications. 

The authors utilized a review methodology, synthesizing findings from recent studies and large-scale microbiome projects, such as the Human Microbiome Project and MetaHIT, which employed advanced sequencing techniques to analyze gut microbiota composition and function. They also discussed experimental models, including humanized gnotobiotic mice, to investigate the effects of microbiome alterations on health.

Key findings indicate that gut microbiota play crucial roles in host metabolism, immune regulation, and protection against pathogens. Dysbiosis, or microbial imbalance, is linked to various diseases, including Clostridium difficile infection, inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, and autism spectrum disorder. The review highlights how microbial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, influence host physiological processes and immune responses.

In conclusion, the authors suggest that understanding the intricate relationship between gut microbiota and host health could lead to novel microbiome-based therapies, such as fecal microbiota transplantation and probiotics, to restore microbial balance and ameliorate disease symptoms. They also identify significant research gaps, advocating for further studies to elucidate the mechanisms underlying microbiome-host interactions and their implications for health and disease management.

title: Nutrition intervention strategies in chronically malnourished regions: preventing endemic goitre in Togo
abstract: Iodine deficiency disorders (IDDs) are an important problem in the world. Some 760 million people suffer from goitre and 1600 million are at risk. In Togo, a small West African country, the prevalence of visible goitre in 6±12-year-old children was 21.6% and 5.3% in two endemic regions in 1999. The aim of this paper is to describe the procedures followed and key results of a school-based nutrition education project implemented in Togo to prevent iodine deficiency disorders, by encouraging use of iodised salt.
summary:
The main objective of the paper is to describe a school-based nutrition education project in Togo aimed at preventing iodine deficiency disorders (IDDs), particularly endemic goitre, by promoting the use of iodised salt. The study addresses the high prevalence of goitre among children in Togo, where visible goitre rates were reported at 21.6% in 1999.

The methods employed included a comparison of three educational approaches tailored to Togolese culture: puppet performances, oral storytelling, and the use of picture discs/flip charts. The project targeted fourth and sixth-year primary school children across 32 schools in two regions of Togo. A Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices (KAP) survey was conducted before and after the intervention to assess the effectiveness of each educational method.

Key findings revealed that all three methods significantly increased knowledge about iodine and iodised salt among the children. The puppet performance was particularly effective for younger students, while oral storytelling was more beneficial for older pupils. After the intervention, 84.1% of participants reported using iodised salt at home, a substantial increase from 7.5% prior to the project.

In conclusion, the study highlights the importance of culturally adapted nutrition education in combating IDDs. It suggests that a combination of traditional and modern educational methods can effectively raise awareness and change behaviors regarding iodine consumption. The findings imply that similar interventions could be beneficial in other regions facing iodine deficiency, emphasizing the need for ongoing education and community engagement to sustain improvements in public health nutrition.

title: The gut microbiome in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
abstract: The gut microbiota has been linked to cardiovascular diseases. However, the composition and functional capacity of the gut microbiome in relation to cardiovascular diseases have not been systematically examined. Here, we perform a metagenome-wide association study on stools from 218 individuals with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACVD) and 187 healthy controls. The ACVD gut microbiome deviates from the healthy status by increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae and Streptococcus spp. and, functionally, in the potential for metabolism or transport of several molecules important for cardiovascular health. Although drug treatment represents a confounding factor, ACVD status, and not current drug use, is the major distinguishing feature in this cohort. We identify common themes by comparison with gut microbiome data associated with other cardiometabolic diseases (obesity and type 2 diabetes), with liver cirrhosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Our data represent a comprehensive resource for further investigations on the role of the gut microbiome in promoting or preventing ACVD as well as other related diseases.
summary:
The main objective of this study was to investigate the composition and functional capacity of the gut microbiome in individuals with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACVD) compared to healthy controls. The researchers conducted a metagenome-wide association study (MWAS) using stool samples from 218 ACVD patients and 187 healthy individuals.

The methodology involved metagenomic shotgun sequencing of fecal samples, allowing for detailed analysis of microbial composition and functional potential. The study identified significant differences in gut microbiome profiles between ACVD patients and healthy controls, including an increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae and Streptococcus spp. in ACVD patients, alongside functional alterations related to metabolism and transport of cardiovascular health-related molecules.

Key findings revealed that the gut microbiome of ACVD patients exhibited a less diverse and more inflammatory profile, with notable depletion of beneficial bacteria such as butyrate-producing species. Additionally, a random forest classifier demonstrated a high diagnostic potential for distinguishing ACVD patients from healthy individuals based on microbiome composition, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86.

The study concludes that the gut microbiome plays a significant role in ACVD, with potential implications for developing non-invasive biomarkers for diagnosis and understanding the disease's underlying mechanisms. The findings suggest that further research could explore the gut microbiome's role in promoting or preventing ACVD and other related cardiometabolic diseases, highlighting the importance of gut health in cardiovascular conditions.

title: Adherence to Mediterranean diet and health status: meta-analysis
abstract: To systematically review all the prospective cohort studies that have analysed the relation between adherence to a Mediterranean diet, mortality, and incidence of chronic diseases in a primary prevention setting. The cumulative analysis among eight cohorts evaluating overall mortality in relation to adherence to a Mediterranean diet showed that a two point increase in the adherence score was significantly associated with a reduced risk of mortality. Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with a significant improvement in health status, as seen by a significant reduction in overall mortality and incidence of major chronic diseases.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Sofi et al. was to systematically review and meta-analyze prospective cohort studies examining the relationship between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and health outcomes, specifically mortality and incidence of chronic diseases, in a primary prevention context.

The researchers conducted a meta-analysis of 12 prospective cohort studies, which included a total of 1,574,299 participants followed for 3 to 18 years. They utilized databases such as PubMed and Embase to gather relevant studies and assessed the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and various health outcomes, including overall mortality, cardiovascular mortality, cancer incidence/mortality, and incidence of neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

Key findings indicated that a two-point increase in adherence to a Mediterranean diet was significantly associated with a 9% reduction in overall mortality, a 9% reduction in cardiovascular mortality, a 6% reduction in cancer incidence/mortality, and a 13% reduction in the incidence of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases. The results demonstrated consistent benefits across various cohorts, with significant reductions in health risks associated with higher adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern.

In conclusion, the study highlights that greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet is linked to improved health outcomes and reduced mortality risk. These findings underscore the importance of promoting a Mediterranean-like dietary pattern as a public health strategy for the primary prevention of major chronic diseases, aligning with current dietary guidelines from health organizations.

filename: A Review of Micronutrients and the Immune System-Working in Harmony to Reduce th.pdf
title: A Review of Micronutrients and the Immune System–Working in Harmony to Reduce the Risk of Infection
abstract: Immune support by micronutrients is historically based on vitamin C deficiency and supplementation in scurvy in early times. It has since been established that the complex, integrated immune system needs multiple specific micronutrients, including vitamins A, D, C, E, B6, and B12, folate, zinc, iron, copper, and selenium, which play vital, often synergistic roles at every stage of the immune response. Adequate amounts are essential to ensure the proper function of physical barriers and immune cells; however, daily micronutrient intakes necessary to support immune function may be higher than current recommended dietary allowances. Certain populations have inadequate dietary micronutrient intakes, and situations with increased requirements (e.g., infection, stress, and pollution) further decrease stores within the body. Several micronutrients may be deficient, and even marginal deficiency may impair immunity. Although contradictory data exist, available evidence indicates that supplementation with multiple micronutrients with immune-supporting roles may modulate immune function and reduce the risk of infection. Micronutrients with the strongest evidence for immune support are vitamins C and D and zinc. Better design of human clinical studies addressing dosage and combinations of micronutrients in different populations are required to substantiate the benefits of micronutrient supplementation against infection.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Gombart et al. is to review the role of various micronutrients in supporting the immune system and reducing the risk of infection. The authors emphasize that multiple micronutrients, including vitamins A, C, D, E, B6, B12, folate, zinc, iron, copper, and selenium, are essential for optimal immune function.

The review synthesizes findings from existing literature, detailing the mechanisms through which these micronutrients contribute to both innate and adaptive immune responses. The authors highlight that adequate intake of these micronutrients is crucial, as deficiencies—even marginal ones—can impair immune function. They also note that certain populations may have inadequate dietary intakes, particularly in situations of increased physiological demand, such as during infections or stress.

Key findings indicate that specific micronutrients like vitamins C and D and zinc have the strongest evidence supporting their roles in enhancing immune function and reducing infection risk. The paper suggests that supplementation with multiple micronutrients may be beneficial, especially in populations at risk of deficiency.

In conclusion, the authors call for better-designed clinical studies to investigate the optimal dosages and combinations of micronutrients for immune support. They emphasize the importance of addressing micronutrient deficiencies to enhance immune health and reduce the risk of infections, highlighting the potential for public health interventions to improve dietary intake of these essential nutrients.

title: Proton pump inhibitors affect the gut microbiome
abstract: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are among the top 10 most widely used drugs in the world. PPI use has been associated with an increased risk of enteric infections, most notably Clostridium difficile. The gut microbiome plays an important role in enteric infections, by resisting or promoting colonisation by pathogens. In this study, we investigated the influence of PPI use on the gut microbiome.
summary:
The main objective of this study was to investigate the impact of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) on the gut microbiome, given their association with increased risks of enteric infections, particularly Clostridium difficile. The researchers analyzed the gut microbiome composition of 1,815 individuals across three cohorts using tag sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene, comparing PPI users to non-users.

Key findings revealed that PPI use significantly decreased microbial diversity and altered the composition of approximately 20% of bacterial taxa. Specifically, there was an overrepresentation of oral bacteria, such as the genus Rothia, and an increase in potentially pathogenic species, including Enterococcus and Escherichia coli, among PPI users. The study also noted that the microbial changes associated with PPI use were more pronounced than those linked to antibiotics or other commonly used medications.

The conclusions drawn from this research suggest that PPI use leads to a less healthy gut microbiome, which may contribute to the heightened risk of enteric infections. The findings underscore the need for healthcare practitioners to consider the effects of PPIs on gut microbiota when prescribing these medications, as the alterations in microbiome composition could facilitate the colonization of pathogens like C. difficile. This study highlights the importance of understanding the broader implications of PPI use on gut health and infection susceptibility.

title: Role of Probiotics in Human Gut Microbiome-Associated Diseases
abstract: In modern times, probiotics have attracted public interest in the course of promoting human intestinal health, and the addition of prebiotics to probiotics, as synbiotics, has also been recommended. Therefore, the global probiotics market has grown rapidly, which makes probiotics not only as a supplement but also a food. The intake of probiotics has been suggested to enhance overall health and immunity. It is now recognized that the human gut microbiota may play a role in the development of metabolic diseases including obesity, diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease. Interestingly, the administration of probiotics has been shown to improve the prognosis and management of those diseases. This review provides a brief summary of the concept and function of probiotics, and their relationship with intestinal microbiome-associated diseases.
summary:
The main objective of the paper is to explore the role of probiotics in managing human gut microbiome-associated diseases, particularly focusing on their effects on conditions like obesity, diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and colorectal cancer (CRC). 

The authors conducted a review of existing literature, including clinical trials and in vivo studies, to assess the impact of probiotics on gut microbiota and related diseases. They examined the definitions, benefits, and mechanisms of probiotics, as well as their potential to restore gut homeostasis disrupted by dysbiosis.

Key findings indicate that probiotics can beneficially influence the gut microbiota, potentially alleviating symptoms of various intestinal disorders. They have shown promise in reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and improving conditions in patients with IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis, although results for Crohn's disease remain inconsistent. Probiotics also exhibit anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties, suggesting they may help in preventing CRC by altering gut microbiota composition.

In conclusion, the paper underscores the significant connection between probiotics and gut health, advocating for their use as adjunct therapies in treating intestinal diseases. However, it also highlights the need for further research to clarify the mechanisms of action and to establish standardized guidelines for probiotic use in clinical settings. The findings suggest that probiotics could be integral to future strategies for preventing and managing gut microbiome-associated diseases, but caution is advised regarding their overuse in vulnerable populations.

filename: The Influence of Probiotics on the Firmicutes_Bacteroidetes Ratio in the Treatme.pdf
title: The Influence of Probiotics on the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes Ratio in the Treatment of Obesity and Inflammatory Bowel Disease
abstract: The two most important bacterial phyla in the gastrointestinal tract, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, have gained much attention in recent years. The Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio is widely accepted to have an important influence in maintaining normal intestinal homeostasis. Increased or decreased F/B ratio is regarded as dysbiosis, whereby the former is usually observed with obesity, and the latter with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Probiotics as live microorganisms can confer health benefits to the host when administered in adequate amounts. There is considerable evidence of their nutritional and immunosuppressive properties including reports that elucidate the association of probiotics with the F/B ratio, obesity, and IBD. Orally administered probiotics can contribute to the restoration of dysbiotic microbiota and to the prevention of obesity or IBD. However, as the effects of different probiotics on the F/B ratio differ, selecting the appropriate species or mixture is crucial. The most commonly tested probiotics for modifying the F/B ratio and treating obesity and IBD are from the genus Lactobacillus. In this paper, we review the effects of probiotics on the F/B ratio that lead to weight loss or immunosuppression.
summary:
The main objective of the review by Stojanov et al. is to explore the influence of probiotics on the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio and their potential in treating obesity and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The authors discuss how dysbiosis, characterized by an altered F/B ratio, is associated with obesity (increased F/B ratio) and IBD (decreased F/B ratio).

The review synthesizes findings from various studies that utilized biochemical and molecular methods, such as 16S rRNA gene amplification, to assess the F/B ratio in different populations. It highlights that probiotics, particularly from the Lactobacillus genus, can modulate the gut microbiota, potentially restoring the F/B ratio and alleviating conditions like obesity and IBD.

Key findings indicate that specific probiotics can decrease the F/B ratio and promote weight loss or reduce inflammation. For instance, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Lactobacillus paracasei HII01 were shown to effectively lower the F/B ratio and improve metabolic parameters in animal models. Conversely, some probiotics may not affect the F/B ratio but still provide benefits, such as weight management.

In conclusion, the review emphasizes the therapeutic potential of probiotics in managing obesity and IBD through modulation of the gut microbiota and F/B ratio. However, it also notes the complexity of individual responses to probiotics, suggesting that personalized approaches may be necessary for effective treatment. The implications of this research could guide future probiotic formulations and dietary interventions aimed at improving gut health and managing obesity and IBD.

title: The Mediterranean diet: health, science and society
abstract: The Mediterranean diet (MD) emerged as a healthy food regimen long before it could be recognised which nutrients or foods were responsible for its observed benefits. Epidemiological and anthropological studies of the MD converged, first by investigating single nutrients or foods, then by adopting a more holistic approach of dietary patterns (DP), and now with a molecular approach. These studies resulted in convincing evidence that a MD decreases the risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality and incidence. A risk reduction of developing type 2 diabetes is probable. Evidence is less stringent for other metabolic diseases and all cancers but from possible to probable for some cancer sites. Although DP showed that the MD has to be considered in its totality, olive oil could have a specific role. Lifestyle factors such as physical activity for energy balance, outdoor life for vitamin D synthesis and conviviality are also probably partly responsible for the health benefits. The MD is a lifestyle well suited for coping not only with personal health but also with wider societal concerns in relation to environment, public health and economy.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Gerber and Hoffman is to explore the health benefits, scientific evidence, and societal implications of the Mediterranean diet (MD). The authors review historical and contemporary studies, including epidemiological and molecular research, to understand the diet's impact on health outcomes.

The methods employed include a comprehensive literature review of historical observations, dietary pattern analyses, and intervention studies, notably the Seven Countries Study and the PREDIMED trial, which assess the relationship between MD adherence and various health metrics.

Key findings indicate that adherence to the MD is associated with a significant reduction in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, as well as a probable decrease in the incidence of type 2 diabetes. The diet's holistic nature, particularly the role of olive oil and lifestyle factors like physical activity and social interactions, contributes to its health benefits. While evidence for its effects on cancer risk is less robust, some studies suggest potential protective effects against certain cancer types.

In conclusion, the authors argue that the MD is not just a dietary regimen but a comprehensive lifestyle that promotes individual health, public health, and environmental sustainability. They emphasize the need for public health initiatives to promote the MD, highlighting its economic advantages in reducing healthcare costs associated with chronic diseases. The paper advocates for a broader understanding of the MD, incorporating its cultural and social dimensions to enhance its adoption and benefits.

title: Microbiome definition re-visited: old concepts and new challenges
abstract: The field of microbiome research has evolved rapidly over the past few decades and has become a topic of great scientific and public interest. As a result of this rapid growth in interest covering different fields, we are lacking a clear commonly agreed definition of the term “microbiome.” Moreover, a consensus on best practices in microbiome research is missing. Recently, a panel of international experts discussed the current gaps in the frame of the European-funded MicrobiomeSupport project. The meeting brought together about 40 leaders from diverse microbiome areas, while more than a hundred experts from all over the world took part in an online survey accompanying the workshop. This article excerpts the outcomes of the workshop and the corresponding online survey embedded in a short historical introduction and future outlook. We propose a definition of microbiome based on the compact, clear, and comprehensive description of the term provided by Whipps et al. in 1988, amended with a set of novel recommendations considering the latest technological developments and research findings.
summary:
The main objective of the paper "Microbiome definition re-visited: old concepts and new challenges" is to establish a clear, comprehensive definition of the term "microbiome" and to address the challenges faced in microbiome research due to the lack of consensus and standardization. 

The authors conducted a workshop with about 40 international experts and an accompanying online survey involving over a hundred participants to gather insights on the definition and challenges in microbiome research. They reviewed historical definitions and proposed an updated definition that incorporates recent technological advancements and research findings, emphasizing the distinction between "microbiome" and "microbiota."

Key findings include the identification of critical aspects of microbiomes, such as the composition and dynamics of microbial communities, the concept of core microbiomes, and the importance of interactions among microbial species and their environments. The authors also highlighted the need for better integration of data and methodologies across different fields of microbiome research.

In conclusion, the paper advocates for a unified definition of microbiome that reflects its complexity and ecological significance. This standardization is crucial for advancing research and applications in various fields, including health, agriculture, and environmental sustainability. The authors emphasize that a clearer understanding of microbiomes can help address anthropogenic challenges, particularly in the context of planetary health.

title: Microbiota in health and diseases
abstract: The role of microbiota in health and diseases is being highlighted by numerous studies since its discovery. Depending on the localized regions, microbiota can be classified into gut, oral, respiratory, and skin microbiota. The microbial communities are in symbiosis with the host, contributing to homeostasis and regulating immune function. However, microbiota dysbiosis can lead to dysregulation of bodily functions and diseases including cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), cancers, respiratory diseases, etc. In this review, we discuss the current knowledge of how microbiota links to host health or pathogenesis.
summary:
The review article "Microbiota in Health and Diseases" by Hou et al. aims to elucidate the role of microbiota in human health and disease, focusing on how microbiota dysbiosis can contribute to various health issues, including cardiovascular diseases, cancers, and respiratory diseases.

The authors employed a comprehensive literature review, summarizing existing research on microbiota in healthy conditions, the mechanisms of dysbiosis in disease development, and clinical approaches for microbiota modulation, such as fecal microbial transplantation.

Key findings indicate that microbiota play crucial roles in maintaining homeostasis, regulating immune functions, and influencing various biological processes. Dysbiosis—characterized by altered microbial community composition—can lead to chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, contributing to disease progression. The review also highlights the gut-brain axis, demonstrating how gut microbiota can affect neurological functions and behaviors.

In conclusion, the authors emphasize the importance of understanding microbiota's role in health and disease, advocating for further research to explore microbiota-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The implications of this work suggest that manipulating microbiota could be a promising avenue for treating various diseases, underscoring the potential for personalized medicine approaches based on individual microbiota profiles.

title: The Impact of Vitamin D Levels on Inflammatory Status: A Systematic Review of Immune Cell Studies
abstract: Chronic low-grade inflammation accompanies obesity and its related chronic conditions. Both peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and cell lines have been used to study whether vitamin D has immune modulating effects; however, to date a detailed systematic review describing the published evidence has not been completed. We therefore conducted a systematic review on the effect of vitamin D on the protein expression and secretion of inflammatory markers by human-derived immune cells. The review was registered at the International Prospective Register for Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, Registration number CRD42015023222). A literature search was conducted using Pubmed, Science Direct, Scopus, Web of Science and Medline. The search strategy used the following search terms: Vitamin D or cholecalciferol or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin or 25-hydroxy-Vitamin D and Inflam* or cytokine* and supplement* or cell*. These terms were searched in the abstract, title and keywords. Inclusion criteria for study selection consisted of human-derived immune cell lines or cellular studies where PBMCs were obtained from humans, reported in the English language, and within the time period of 2000 to 2015. The selection protocol was mapped according to PRISMA guidelines. Twenty three studies (7 cell line and 16 PBMCs studies) met our criteria. All studies selected except one used the active metabolite 1,25(OH)2, with one study using cholecalciferol and two studies also using 25 (OH)D. Four out of seven cell line studies showed an anti-inflammatory effect where suppression of key markers such as macrophage chemotactic protein 1, interleukin 6 and interleukin 8 were observed. Fourteen of sixteen PBMC studies also showed a similar anti-inflammatory effect based on common inflammatory endpoints. Mechanisms for such effects included decreased protein expression of toll-like receptor-2 and toll-like receptor-4; lower levels of phosphorylated p38 and p42/42; reduced expression of phosphorylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 and decreased reactive oxygen species. This review demonstrates that an anti-inflammatory effect of vitamin D is a consistent observation in studies of cell lines and human derived PBMCs.
summary:
The main objective of the research article "The Impact of Vitamin D Levels on Inflammatory Status: A Systematic Review of Immune Cell Studies" was to systematically review the effects of vitamin D on the inflammatory profile of human-derived immune cells, specifically focusing on protein expression and secretion of inflammatory markers.

The authors conducted a systematic literature search across multiple databases (Pubmed, Science Direct, Scopus, Web of Science, and Medline) using specific search terms related to vitamin D and inflammation. They included studies published between 2000 and 2015 that involved human-derived immune cell lines or peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). A total of 23 studies (7 cell line studies and 16 PBMC studies) met the inclusion criteria.

Key findings indicated that vitamin D, particularly in its active form (1,25(OH)2D), consistently exhibited anti-inflammatory effects across both cell lines and PBMCs. Specifically, the studies showed reductions in key inflammatory markers such as interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and macrophage chemotactic protein 1. Mechanisms underlying these effects included decreased expression of toll-like receptors and reduced levels of reactive oxygen species.

In conclusion, the review highlights that vitamin D has a significant anti-inflammatory impact on immune cells, suggesting its potential role in modulating inflammation associated with obesity and chronic diseases. The findings imply that maintaining adequate vitamin D levels could be beneficial for managing inflammatory conditions, warranting further clinical studies to explore vitamin D supplementation as a therapeutic approach for chronic disease prevention.

title: Prebiotic concept and health
abstract: The different compartments of the gastrointestinal tract are inhabited by populations of micro-organisms. By far the most important predominant populations are in the colon where a true symbiosis with the host exists that is a key for well-being and health. For such a microbiota, ‘normobiosis’ characterises a composition of the gut ‘ecosystem’ in which micro-organisms with potential health benefits predominate in number over potentially harmful ones, in contrast to ‘dysbiosis’, in which one or a few potentially harmful micro-organisms are dominant, thus creating a disease-prone situation. The present document has been written by a group of both academic and industry experts (in the ILSI Europe Prebiotic Expert Group and Prebiotic Task Force, respectively). It does not aim to propose a new definition of a prebiotic nor to identify which food products are classified as prebiotic but rather to validate and expand the original idea of the prebiotic concept.
summary:
The main objective of this paper is to validate and expand the concept of prebiotics, defined as substances that selectively stimulate the growth or activity of beneficial gut microorganisms, thereby conferring health benefits to the host. The review synthesizes findings from various studies on the gut microbiota, particularly focusing on the role of prebiotics in promoting a healthy gut environment, termed 'normobiosis,' as opposed to 'dysbiosis,' which is associated with disease.

The authors employed a comprehensive review methodology, analyzing numerous human intervention studies and experimental research that demonstrate the effects of dietary prebiotics on gut microbiota composition and health outcomes. Key findings indicate that the consumption of specific prebiotic food products can significantly increase beneficial bacteria, particularly bifidobacteria, which is linked to improved intestinal health, enhanced immune function, better stool quality, and reduced risks of gastrointestinal infections and allergic conditions.

Conclusions drawn from the review emphasize that prebiotics play a crucial role in modulating gut microbiota, which can lead to various health benefits, including improved metabolic processes related to obesity and type 2 diabetes, enhanced mineral absorption, and potential protective effects against colon cancer. The implications of this research suggest that dietary strategies incorporating prebiotics could be vital in preventing and managing various health conditions, highlighting the importance of gut microbiota in overall well-being. Future research directions are proposed to further explore the mechanisms underlying these health benefits and to identify additional prebiotic candidates.

title: Vitamin D, infections and immunity
abstract: Vitamin D, best known for its role in skeletal health, has emerged as a key regulator of innate immune responses to microbial threat. In immune cells such as macrophages, expression of CYP27B1, the 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1α-hydroxylase, is induced by immune-specific inputs, leading to local production of hormonal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25D) at sites of infection, which in turn directly induces the expression of genes encoding antimicrobial peptides. Vitamin D signaling is active upstream and downstream of pattern recognition receptors, which promote front-line innate immune responses. Moreover, 1,25D stimulates autophagy, which has emerged as a mechanism critical for control of intracellular pathogens such as M. tuberculosis. Strong laboratory and epidemiological evidence links vitamin D deficiency to increased rates of conditions such as dental caries, as well as inflammatory bowel diseases arising from dysregulation of innate immune handling intestinal flora. 1,25D is also active in signaling cascades that promote antiviral innate immunity; 1,25D-induced expression of the antimicrobial peptide CAMP/LL37, originally characterized for its antibacterial properties, is a key component of antiviral responses. Poor vitamin D status is associated with greater susceptibility to viral infections, including those of the respiratory tract. Although the severity of the COVID-19 pandemic has been alleviated in some areas by the arrival of vaccines, it remains important to identify therapeutic interventions that reduce disease severity and mortality, and accelerate recovery. This review outlines of our current knowledge of the mechanisms of action of vitamin D signaling in the innate immune system. It also provides an assessment of the therapeutic potential of vitamin D supplementation in infectious diseases, including an up-to-date analysis of the putative benefits of vitamin D supplementation in the ongoing COVID-19 crisis.
source: Reviews in Endocrine and Metabolic Disorders
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Aiten Ismailova and John H. White is to explore the role of vitamin D in regulating innate immune responses to infections, with a particular focus on its potential therapeutic benefits in infectious diseases, including COVID-19.

The authors utilized a review methodology, synthesizing existing laboratory and epidemiological studies to assess the mechanisms by which vitamin D, specifically its active form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25D), influences immune function. They examined how 1,25D enhances the expression of antimicrobial peptides, stimulates autophagy, and modulates the activity of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) in immune cells.

Key findings indicate that vitamin D deficiency is linked to increased susceptibility to infections, including bacterial and viral pathogens. The review highlights that 1,25D plays a crucial role in promoting both antibacterial and antiviral immunity by regulating gene expression related to innate immune responses. Notably, it enhances the production of antimicrobial peptides like cathelicidin, which has been shown to inhibit viral entry and replication, including against SARS-CoV-2.

The authors conclude that adequate vitamin D levels are essential for optimal immune function and suggest that vitamin D supplementation could be a valuable therapeutic strategy to mitigate the severity of infections, particularly in populations at risk for deficiency. This has significant implications for public health, especially in the context of ongoing viral outbreaks like COVID-19, where vitamin D status may influence disease outcomes.

title: Selective manipulation of the gut microbiota improves immune status in vertebrates
abstract: This review summarizes the mechanisms by which selective manipulation of the gut microbiota can improve immune status in vertebrates, particularly focusing on the roles of probiotics, prebiotics, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in enhancing host health and resistance against pathogens.
summary:
The main objective of the paper "Selective manipulation of the gut microbiota improves immune status in vertebrates" is to explore how dietary strategies, particularly the use of probiotics and prebiotics, can manipulate gut microbiota to enhance immune health in vertebrates, with a focus on fish.

The authors employed a review methodology, synthesizing existing research on the role of gut microbiota in health and disease across various vertebrate models, including fish. They examined the mechanisms by which probiotics (live microorganisms) and prebiotics (non-digestible food ingredients) influence gut microbiota composition and immune responses, particularly through the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs).

Key findings indicate that selective manipulation of gut microbiota through dietary interventions can improve immune responses and resistance to pathogens, especially during stress. The review highlights the importance of SCFAs as metabolites that mediate beneficial effects on the host's immune system. It also notes that while the mechanisms of action for probiotics and prebiotics are still debated, their potential to restore gut health and prevent dysbiosis is well-supported.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the therapeutic potential of dietary strategies in modulating gut microbiota to enhance health in vertebrates. The findings suggest that further research into the gut microbiome, particularly in fish, could lead to innovative approaches for improving health and disease resistance, thereby reducing reliance on antibiotics and chemical treatments in aquaculture and other veterinary practices.

title: Characterization of the Gut Microbiome Using 16S or Shotgun Metagenomics
abstract: The advent of next generation sequencing (NGS) has enabled investigations of the gut microbiome with unprecedented resolution and throughput. This has stimulated the development of sophisticated bioinformatics tools to analyze the massive amounts of data generated. Researchers therefore need a clear understanding of the key concepts required for the design, execution and interpretation of NGS experiments on microbiomes. We conducted a literature review and used our own data to determine which approaches work best. The two main approaches for analyzing the microbiome, 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicons and shotgun metagenomics, are illustrated with analyses of libraries designed to highlight their strengths and weaknesses. Several methods for taxonomic classification of bacterial sequences are discussed. We present simulations to assess the number of sequences that are required to perform reliable appraisals of bacterial community structure. To the extent that fluctuations in the diversity of gut bacterial populations correlate with health and disease, we emphasize various techniques for the analysis of bacterial communities within samples (α-diversity) and between samples (β-diversity). Finally, we demonstrate techniques to infer the metabolic capabilities of a bacteria community from these 16S and shotgun data.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Jovel et al. (2016) is to compare two primary methods for characterizing the gut microbiome—16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomics—while providing insights into their strengths, weaknesses, and best practices for analysis.

The authors conducted a literature review and utilized their own datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of these methods. They performed taxonomic classification of bacterial sequences, assessed bacterial diversity (α-diversity and β-diversity), and inferred the metabolic capabilities of bacterial communities. Simulations were used to determine the necessary sequencing depth for reliable community structure assessments.

Key findings include that while both methods can yield similar results at the genus level, shotgun metagenomics generally offers greater resolution for species identification. The study also highlights the importance of sequencing quality and depth, revealing that higher sequencing depths improve the accuracy of taxonomic classifications. The authors found that biases in 16S rRNA sequencing can lead to overrepresentation of certain genera, complicating accurate community profiling.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the need for careful consideration of sequencing methods and bioinformatics tools when analyzing gut microbiome data. The insights provided can guide researchers in selecting appropriate methodologies for their studies, ultimately enhancing our understanding of the gut microbiome's role in health and disease. The findings underscore the potential for improved diagnostics and therapeutic strategies based on microbiome analysis.

title: New hypotheses for the health-protective mechanisms of whole-grain cereals: what is beyond fibre?
abstract: Epidemiological studies have clearly shown that whole-grain cereals can protect against obesity, diabetes, CVD and cancers. The specific effects of food structure, fibre, and various bioactive compounds are well-recognised mechanisms in this protection. Recent findings have led to new hypotheses regarding the involvement of polyphenols, sulfur compounds, and other components in antioxidant protection. The paper discusses the potential protective effects of various compounds found in whole-grain wheat and the importance of studying their physiological mechanisms.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Anthony Fardet is to explore and propose new hypotheses regarding the health-protective mechanisms of whole-grain cereals, particularly focusing on whole-grain wheat. The research aims to identify the physiological mechanisms that contribute to the protective effects against chronic diseases such as obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and cancer.

To achieve this, the author conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature, detailing the bioactive compounds found in whole-grain wheat, including their distribution in the bran and germ fractions, and their estimated bioavailability. The paper discusses recognized mechanisms such as the role of dietary fiber, food structure, and various bioactive compounds (e.g., polyphenols, vitamins, and minerals) in promoting health.

Key findings indicate that whole-grain wheat contains a diverse array of bioactive compounds that contribute to its health benefits. These compounds are involved in various physiological functions, including antioxidant activity, anti-inflammatory effects, and regulation of gene expression. The study highlights the importance of the synergistic effects of these compounds and the influence of the cereal matrix on their bioavailability and physiological impact.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the need for further research to elucidate the complex interactions of bioactive compounds in whole grains and their collective impact on health. The implications of this research suggest that improving the nutritional quality of cereal products could enhance their protective properties, thereby contributing to better public health outcomes. The author advocates for a nutrigenomic approach to deepen understanding of these mechanisms and to optimize whole-grain consumption for health benefits.

title: Health effects of whole grains
abstract: Epidemiological studies find that whole-grain intake is protective against cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and obesity. Potential mechanisms for this protection are diverse since whole grains are rich in nutrients and phytochemicals. This paper reviews four mechanisms that have been studied for the protectiveness of whole grains: large-bowel effects, glucose and insulin changes, antioxidant theory, and other bioactive compounds.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Joanne Slavin is to explore the health benefits of whole grains and the biological mechanisms that contribute to their protective effects against chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and obesity.

To achieve this, the author reviews existing epidemiological studies and mechanistic research on whole grains, highlighting their rich content of dietary fiber, resistant starch, oligosaccharides, antioxidants, and various bioactive compounds. The paper discusses four primary mechanisms: the effects of whole grains on gut health, their influence on glucose and insulin metabolism, the role of antioxidants in disease prevention, and the presence of other beneficial compounds like lignans and phytosterols.

Key findings indicate that whole grains improve biomarkers associated with health, such as insulin sensitivity, blood lipid levels, and antioxidant protection. The consumption of whole grains is linked to lower glycemic responses and may enhance gut fermentation, leading to the production of short-chain fatty acids that benefit colon health. Additionally, the synergistic effects of the various compounds in whole grains appear to provide greater health benefits than isolated nutrients.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the need for increased public awareness regarding whole grain consumption and the importance of identifying the most protective components within whole grains. The findings suggest that promoting whole grain intake could significantly contribute to reducing the risk of chronic diseases, highlighting the necessity for further research on the physiological effects of whole grains in human diets.

title: Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
abstract: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), one of the most common metabolic disorders, is caused by a combination of two primary factors: defective insulin secretion by pancreatic β-cells and the inability of insulin-sensitive tissues to respond appropriately to insulin. Because insulin release and activity are essential processes for glucose homeostasis, the molecular mechanisms involved in the synthesis and release of insulin, as well as in its detection are tightly regulated. Defects in any of the mechanisms involved in these processes can lead to a metabolic imbalance responsible for the development of the disease. This review analyzes the key aspects of T2DM, as well as the molecular mechanisms and pathways implicated in insulin metabolism leading to T2DM and insulin resistance.
summary:
The paper titled "Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus" aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms and pathways involved in the development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), focusing on insulin metabolism and its relationship with insulin resistance (IR) and cardiovascular complications.

The authors conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature, analyzing key aspects of T2DM, including insulin synthesis, release, sensing, and the impact of various pathological conditions such as obesity, physical inactivity, gut dysbiosis, and metabolic memory. They also examined the epidemiology of T2DM, highlighting the significant global rise in incidence, particularly in low-to-middle-income countries.

Key findings indicate that T2DM is primarily driven by defective insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells and the inability of insulin-sensitive tissues to respond to insulin. The review identifies obesity as the strongest risk factor, with mechanisms including inflammation and oxidative stress contributing to IR. Additionally, the interplay between genetic predispositions and environmental factors is emphasized, suggesting that lifestyle modifications could mitigate T2DM risk.

The authors conclude that T2DM is a complex disorder influenced by a myriad of factors, necessitating a multifaceted approach for prevention and treatment. Understanding the intricate pathophysiological mechanisms is crucial for developing targeted therapies and public health strategies to combat the growing T2DM epidemic. The implications of this research underscore the importance of addressing modifiable risk factors and enhancing awareness of the disease's multifactorial nature to improve patient outcomes.

title: Host Energy Regulation via SCFAs Receptors, as Dietary Nutrition Sensors, by Gut Microbiota
abstract: Food intake regulates energy balance, and its dysregulation leads to metabolic disorders such as obesity and diabetes. Free fatty acids are not only essential nutrients but also act as signaling molecules in various cellular processes. Recent studies have shown that the receptors GPR40, GPR41, GPR43, and GPR120 are new drug targets for treating metabolic disorders because they are activated by free fatty acids. Two of these receptors, GPR41 and GPR43, are activated by short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs: acetate, propionate, and butyrate), which are important energy sources for the host. During feeding, SCFAs are produced by the microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the gut. The gut microbiota affect nutrient acquisition and energy regulation of the host, and can influence the development of obesity, insulin resistance, and diabetes. Hence, GPR41 and GPR43 are also a focus of research into energy regulation via SCFAs.
summary:
The main objective of this paper by Ikuo Kimura is to elucidate the mechanisms by which gut microbiota, through short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and their receptors (GPR41 and GPR43), regulate host energy homeostasis and contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity and diabetes.

The research employs a combination of genetic knockout models (Gpr41KO and Gpr43KO mice) and various biochemical assays to investigate the roles of GPR41 and GPR43 in energy regulation.
