The study focuses on how these receptors respond to SCFAs produced during the fermentation of dietary fibers by gut bacteria, influencing sympathetic nervous system activity and insulin signaling in adipose tissue.

Key findings indicate that GPR41 enhances sympathetic activity in response to SCFAs, promoting energy expenditure, while GPR43 modulates insulin signaling in adipose tissue, preventing excessive fat accumulation. The activation of these receptors plays a crucial role in maintaining energy balance, with GPR41 directly regulating sympathetic nerve activity and GPR43 selectively inhibiting insulin effects in fat tissue.

In conclusion, the study highlights the significant role of gut microbiota-derived SCFAs in energy homeostasis through the action of GPR41 and GPR43. These findings suggest potential therapeutic targets for metabolic disorders, emphasizing the importance of gut microbiota in energy regulation and the development of probiotics as a strategy for preventing lifestyle-related diseases. Further research is needed to explore the interactions of these receptors and their broader implications in metabolic health.

title: Genomic Effects of the Vitamin D Receptor: Potentially the Link between Vitamin D, Immune Cells, and Multiple Sclerosis
abstract: Vitamin D has a plethora of functions that are important for the maintenance of general health and in particular, the functional integrity of the immune system, such as promoting an anti-inflammatory cytokine profile and reducing the Treg/Th17 ratio. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative central nervous system (CNS) disorder of probable autoimmune origin. MS is characterized by recurring or progressive demyelination and degeneration of the CNS due in part to a misguided immune response to as yet undefined (CNS) antigens, potentially including myelin basic protein and proteolipid protein. MS has also been shown to be associated significantly with environmental factors such as the lack of vitamin D. The role of vitamin D in the pathogenesis and progression of MS is complex. Recent genetic studies have shown that various common MS-associated risk-single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are located within or in the vicinity of genes associated with the complex metabolism of vitamin D. The functional aspects of these genetic associations may be explained either by a direct SNP-associated loss- or gain-of-function in a vitamin D-associated gene or due to a change in the regulation of gene expression in certain immune cell types. The development of new genetic tools using next-generation sequencing: e.g., chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and the accompanying rapid progress of epigenomics has made it possible to recognize that the association between vitamin D and MS could be based on the extensive and characteristic genomic binding of the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Therefore, it is important to analyze comprehensively the spatiotemporal VDR binding patterns that have been identified using ChIP-seq in multiple immune cell types to reveal an integral profile of genomic VDR interaction. In summary, the aim of this review is to connect genomic effects vitamin D has on immune cells with MS and thus, to contribute to a better understanding of the influence of vitamin D on the etiology and the pathogenesis of this complex autoimmune disease.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Lu, Taylor, and Körner (2018) is to explore the genomic effects of the vitamin D receptor (VDR) and its potential link to immune cell function and the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS). The authors aim to connect the role of vitamin D in immune regulation with its association with MS, a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and neurodegeneration.

The methods employed include a comprehensive review of existing literature, particularly focusing on genetic studies that identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) related to vitamin D metabolism and their implications for MS risk. The authors also discuss advanced genomic techniques, such as chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq), to analyze VDR binding patterns in various immune cell types.

Key findings indicate that vitamin D plays a crucial role in modulating immune responses, particularly by influencing the balance between pro-inflammatory Th17 cells and regulatory T cells (Tregs). The paper highlights that genetic variations in vitamin D metabolism genes are associated with MS risk and that VDR binding sites are prevalent in regions linked to immune function. The authors also note that vitamin D supplementation may have protective effects against MS clinical activity, although the precise mechanisms remain complex and multifaceted.

In conclusion, the study emphasizes the importance of understanding the genomic interactions of VDR in immune cells to elucidate the etiology of MS. The findings suggest that vitamin D status and its metabolic pathways could be critical factors in MS risk and progression, highlighting the need for further research into vitamin D's therapeutic potential in autoimmune diseases.

title: Vitamin D and the Immune System
abstract: Evidence of the role of vitamin D in the regulation of T and B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and keratinocytes continues to accumulate and provides a link between vitamin D and many autoimmune diseases, including Crohn’s disease, juvenile diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, asthma, and rheumatoid arthritis. Considering the influence of vitamin D on the immune system, it may have potential as a treatment for immune-mediated diseases, even if additional research is required to better quantify dosage. But the biggest obstacle to its clinical use is its potent hypercalcemic effect. The calcium status of the host may influence the effect of vitamin D on immunity.
summary:
The paper by Maruotti and Cantatore explores the relationship between vitamin D and the immune system, particularly its potential role in regulating autoimmune diseases such as Crohn's disease, multiple sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. The main objective is to understand how vitamin D influences immune cell function and its implications for treating immune-mediated diseases.

The authors review existing literature and studies that demonstrate vitamin D's effects on various immune cells, including T and B lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. They highlight that vitamin D acts through its receptor (VDR) to modulate immune responses, inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines (like IL-2 and IFN-γ) and promoting anti-inflammatory cytokines (like IL-4 and IL-10). They also discuss the role of vitamin D in enhancing regulatory T cells and its impact on dendritic cell differentiation.

Key findings indicate that vitamin D deficiency is linked to several autoimmune diseases, and adequate levels may help mitigate disease severity. However, the clinical application of vitamin D is limited by its hypercalcemic effects and the need for further research to determine optimal dosing.

In conclusion, the authors suggest that vitamin D has significant immunoregulatory properties that could be harnessed in treating autoimmune conditions. They emphasize the need for more studies to quantify effective dosages and to understand the interplay between vitamin D and calcium in immune regulation, which could pave the way for new therapeutic strategies in managing autoimmune diseases.

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Antioxidants in Edible Wild Plants
abstract: Human beings evolved on a diet that was balanced in the omega-6 and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), and was high in antioxidants. Edible wild plants provide alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and higher amounts of vitamin E and vitamin C than cultivated plants. In addition to the antioxidant vitamins, edible wild plants are rich in phenols and other compounds that increase their antioxidant capacity. It is therefore important to systematically analyze the total antioxidant capacity of wild plants and promote their commercialization in both developed and developing countries.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Artemis P. Simopoulos is to analyze the omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidant content in edible wild plants, emphasizing their potential health benefits compared to cultivated plants. The research highlights the evolutionary dietary patterns of humans, which included a balanced intake of omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids and a high consumption of antioxidants.

The methods employed include systematic analysis of the antioxidant capacity of various wild plants, particularly focusing on alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and its conversion to long-chain omega-3 fatty acids. The study compares the nutritional profiles of wild plants, such as purslane, with cultivated varieties, assessing their contents of vitamins E and C, phenols, and other antioxidants.

Key findings indicate that edible wild plants contain significantly higher levels of ALA and antioxidants than cultivated plants. For instance, purslane was found to be a rich source of omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants, surpassing common vegetables in these nutrients. The paper also discusses the adverse effects of high linoleic acid intake prevalent in Western diets, which can lead to increased oxidative stress and health risks, contrasting with the protective effects of ALA.

In conclusion, the study advocates for the promotion and commercialization of edible wild plants as a means to improve dietary omega-3 fatty acid and antioxidant intake. This could have significant implications for public health, particularly in preventing chronic diseases such as coronary heart disease, hypertension, and cancer, by encouraging a return to more traditional, diverse diets rich in wild plant sources.

title: Beneficial effects on host energy metabolism of short‑chain fatty acids and vitamins produced by commensal and probiotic bacteria
abstract: The aim of this review is to summarize the effect in host energy metabolism of the production of B group vitamins and short chain fatty acids (SCFA) by commensal, food-grade and probiotic bacteria, which are also actors of the mammalian nutrition. The mechanisms of how these microbial end products, produced by these bacterial strains, act on energy metabolism will be discussed. We will show that these vitamins and SCFA producing bacteria could be used as tools to recover energy intakes by either optimizing ATP production from foods or by the fermentation of certain fibers in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT).
summary:
The review by LeBlanc et al. (2017) aims to summarize the effects of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and B group vitamins produced by commensal and probiotic bacteria on host energy metabolism. The authors discuss the mechanisms through which these microbial products influence energy production, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract.

The methods employed include a review of existing literature and original data on SCFA and vitamin production by selected probiotic strains. The authors highlight the role of SCFAs—specifically acetate, propionate, and butyrate—as metabolic fuels that contribute significantly to the host's energy needs, potentially providing up to 10% of daily caloric requirements. They also evaluate the capacity of various probiotic strains to produce B vitamins, which serve as essential cofactors in energy metabolism.

Key findings indicate that SCFAs and B vitamins produced by gut microbiota play crucial roles in energy metabolism, influencing processes such as glucose synthesis and lipid metabolism. The review emphasizes that butyrate is particularly important for colonic epithelial energy, while acetate and propionate are utilized by peripheral tissues. Furthermore, the authors note that the presence of these metabolites can affect the host's metabolic profile and may be linked to conditions like obesity and diabetes.

In conclusion, the authors suggest that enhancing the production of SCFAs and B vitamins through dietary interventions or probiotics could improve energy metabolism and potentially alleviate fatigue. They call for further clinical studies to explore the relationship between gut microbiota, energy metabolites, and fatigue in humans, highlighting the therapeutic potential of probiotics in managing energy-related disorders.

filename: Vitamin D deficiency 2_0_ an update on the current status worldwide_.pdf
title: Vitamin D deficiency 2.0: an update on the current status worldwide
abstract: Vitamin D testing and the use of vitamin D supplements have increased substantially in recent years. Currently, the role of vitamin D supplementation, and the optimal vitamin D dose and status, is a subject of debate, because large interventional studies have been unable to show a clear benefit (in mostly vitamin D replete populations). This may be attributed to limitations in trial design, as most studies did not meet the basic requirements of a nutrient intervention study, including vitamin D-replete populations, too small sample sizes, and inconsistent intervention methods regarding dose and metabolites. Vitamin D deficiency (serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] < 50 nmol/L or 20 ng/ml) is associated with unfavorable skeletal outcomes, including fractures and bone loss. A 25(OH)D level of >50 nmol/L or 20 ng/ml is, therefore, the primary treatment goal, although some data suggest a benefit for a higher threshold. Severe vitamin D deficiency with a 25(OH)D concentration below <30 nmol/L (or 12 ng/ml) dramatically increases the risk of excess mortality, infections, and many other diseases, and should be avoided whenever possible. The data on a benefit for mortality and prevention of infections, at least in severely deficient individuals, appear convincing. Vitamin D is clearly not a panacea, and is most likely efficient only in deficiency. Given its rare side effects and its relatively wide safety margin, it may be an important, inexpensive, and safe adjuvant therapy for many diseases, but future large and well-designed studies should evaluate this further. A worldwide public health intervention that includes vitamin D supplementation in certain risk groups, and systematic vitamin D food fortification to avoid severe vitamin D deficiency, would appear to be important.
summary:
The main objective of the review article "Vitamin D deficiency 2.0: an update on the current status worldwide" is to assess the global prevalence of vitamin D deficiency, its health implications, and the effectiveness of vitamin D supplementation. The authors highlight the ongoing debate regarding optimal vitamin D levels and the benefits of supplementation, particularly in populations that are vitamin D deficient.

The methods employed in this narrative review included a comprehensive literature search in PubMed for relevant studies up to October 2019, focusing on large observational and interventional studies related to vitamin D.

Key findings indicate that approximately 40% of Europeans and significant portions of populations in other regions, such as India and Tunisia, are vitamin D deficient. Severe deficiency (<30 nmol/L) is linked to increased risks of mortality, infections, and various diseases. The review critiques many interventional studies for including non-deficient populations and lacking proper design, which may explain their failure to demonstrate clear benefits of supplementation.

In conclusion, while vitamin D is not a cure-all, it is essential for preventing severe deficiency and associated health risks. The authors advocate for public health interventions, including targeted supplementation for at-risk groups and food fortification, to combat vitamin D deficiency globally. They call for future well-designed studies to better evaluate the role of vitamin D supplementation, particularly in deficient populations, to clarify its potential health benefits.

title: The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics consensus statement on the scope and appropriate use of the term probiotic
abstract: An expert panel was convened in October 2013 by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) to discuss the field of probiotics. It is now 13 years since the definition of probiotics and 12 years after guidelines were published for regulators, scientists and industry by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the WHO (FAO/WHO). The FAO/WHO definition of a probiotic—'live microorganisms which when administered in adequate amounts confer a health benefit on the host'—was reinforced as relevant and sufficiently accommodating for current and anticipated applications. However, inconsistencies between the FAO/WHO Expert Consultation Report and the FAO/WHO Guidelines were clarified to take into account advances in science and applications. A more precise use of the term ‘probiotic’ will be useful to guide clinicians and consumers in differentiating the diverse products on the market. This document represents the conclusions of the ISAPP consensus meeting on the appropriate use and scope of the term probiotic.
summary:
**Main Objective/Research Question:**  
The paper presents the consensus statement from an expert panel convened by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) to clarify the definition and appropriate use of the term "probiotic" in light of advancements in science and the growing market of probiotic products.

**Methods Used:**  
The panel consisted of international experts in various fields related to probiotics. They discussed key questions regarding the definition and classification of probiotics, reviewed existing literature, and achieved a unanimous consensus on the outcomes, which were compiled into a draft report for publication.

**Key Findings:**  
The panel reaffirmed the FAO/WHO definition of probiotics as "live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host," with minor grammatical adjustments. They identified core benefits associated with certain well-studied probiotic species, such as supporting gut health and immune function. The panel also highlighted issues of misuse of the term "probiotic" in marketing and emphasized the need for clearer guidelines to differentiate legitimate probiotic products from those lacking scientific backing.

**Conclusions and Implications:**  
The consensus statement aims to provide stakeholders—including consumers, researchers, health professionals, and industry—with clearer guidelines for defining and using probiotics. It stresses the importance of substantiating health claims with scientific evidence and proposes a framework for evaluating probiotics based on their health benefits. This effort seeks to enhance consumer protection and promote informed decision-making regarding probiotic products, ultimately benefiting public health through better understanding and application of probiotics.

title: Differences in immune status and fecal SCFA between Indonesian stunted children and children with normal nutritional status
abstract: We recently showed that the gut microbiota composition of stunted children was different from that of children with normal nutritional status. Here, we compared immune status and fecal microbial metabolite concentrations between stunted and normal children, and we correlated macronutrient intake (including energy), metabolites and immune status to microbiota composition. The results show that macronutrient intake was lower in stunted children for all components, but after correction for multiple comparison significant only for energy and fat. Only TGF-β was significantly different between stunted children and children of normal nutritional status after correction for multiple comparisons. TNF-alpha, IL-10, lipopolysaccharide binding protein in serum and secretory IgA in feces were not significantly different. Strikingly, all the individual short-chain and branched-chain fatty acids were higher in fecal samples of stunted children (significant for acetate, valerate and total SCFA). These metabolites correlated with a number of different microbial taxa, but due to extensive cross-feeding between microbes, did not show a specific pattern. However, the energy-loss due to higher excretion in stunted children of these metabolites, which can be used as substrate for the host, is striking. Several microbial taxa also correlated to the intake of macronutrients (including dietary fibre) and energy. Eisenbergiella positively correlated with all macronutrients, while an uncharacterized genus within the Succinivibrionaceae family negatively correlated with all macronutrients. These, and the other correlations observed, may provide indication on how to modulate the gut microbiota of stunted children such that their growth lag can be corrected.
summary:
The study aimed to investigate the differences in immune status and fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) between stunted Indonesian children and those with normal nutritional status, while also examining the correlations between macronutrient intake, microbial metabolites, and gut microbiota composition.

A cross-sectional study was conducted involving 78 stunted children and 53 children with normal nutritional status, aged 3-5 years. Researchers assessed dietary intake through 24-hour food recalls, collected blood and stool samples, and measured various immune parameters (e.g., TGF-β, IL-10, TNF-α) and SCFA concentrations using ELISA and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS).

Key findings revealed that stunted children had significantly lower energy and fat intake compared to their normal counterparts. While TGF-β levels were higher in stunted children, other immune markers (IL-10, TNF-α, lipopolysaccharide binding protein, and secretory IgA) showed no significant differences. Notably, fecal SCFA concentrations, particularly acetate, valerate, and total SCFA, were higher in stunted children, suggesting altered gut microbiota metabolism. The study also identified correlations between specific microbial taxa and macronutrient intake.

The study concludes that the higher SCFA levels in stunted children may reflect an adaptive response to their nutritional status, potentially contributing to an anti-inflammatory effect. However, the increased excretion of SCFAs could also lead to energy loss, exacerbating growth issues. These findings imply that modulating gut microbiota through dietary interventions could help address stunting and improve nutritional outcomes in affected populations.

title: Human-origin probiotic cocktail increases short-chain fatty acid production via modulation of mice and human gut microbiome
abstract: The gut bacteria producing metabolites like short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs; e.g., acetate, propionate and butyrate), are frequently reduced in Patients with diabetes, obesity, autoimmune disorders, and cancers. Hence, microbiome modulators such as probiotics may be helpful in maintaining or even restoring normal gut microbiome composition to benefit host health. Herein, we developed a human-origin probiotic cocktail with the ability to modulate gut microbiota to increase native SCFA production. Following a robust protocol of isolation, characterization and safety validation of infant gut-origin Lactobacillus and Enterococcus strains with probiotic attributes, we select 10 strains (5 from each genera) out of total 321 isolates. A single dose (oral gavage) as well as 5 consecutive doses of this 10-strain probiotic cocktail in mice modulates gut microbiome and increases SCFA production (particularly propionate and butyrate). Inoculation of these probiotics in human feces also increases SCFA production along with microbiome modulation. Results indicate that human-origin probiotic lactobacilli and enterococci could ameliorate gut microbiome dysbiosis and hence may prove to be a potential therapy for diseases involving reduced SCFAs production in the gut.
summary:
The main objective of this study was to develop a human-origin probiotic cocktail to modulate gut microbiota and enhance the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in both mice and human fecal samples. The researchers isolated and characterized 321 strains of Lactobacillus and Enterococcus from infant gut samples, ultimately selecting 10 strains based on their probiotic attributes, including tolerance to gastrointestinal conditions and absence of virulence factors.

The study employed both in vivo (mice) and ex vivo (human feces) methods to assess the effects of the probiotic cocktail. Mice were administered either a single dose or five consecutive doses of the probiotic cocktail, and changes in gut microbiome composition and SCFA production were measured over time. In human fecal samples, the probiotic strains were inoculated and incubated to evaluate their impact on microbiome diversity and SCFA levels.

Key findings indicated that the probiotic cocktail significantly increased SCFA production, particularly propionate and butyrate, in both mice and human feces. The treatment also modulated the gut microbiome composition, increasing the abundance of beneficial bacteria such as Bacteroidetes while decreasing Firmicutes. The effects were more pronounced with multiple doses, leading to sustained changes in microbiome diversity and SCFA levels.

In conclusion, the study suggests that the developed human-origin probiotic cocktail could serve as a potential therapeutic approach for conditions associated with reduced SCFA production and gut dysbiosis. The findings highlight the importance of probiotics in restoring gut health and their potential role in managing metabolic and inflammatory diseases.

title: Vitamin D and immunity
abstract: Vitamin D deficiency has been linked to an increased risk of a wide range of adverse health outcomes. The active form of vitamin D has an important role in calcium metabolism and in bone mineralisation, but the evidence for other health outcomes is mixed, with the strongest effects seen in the weakest epidemiological study designs. There are plausible pathways whereby vitamin D deficiency can impair immune function, resulting in both overactivity and increased risk of autoimmune disease, as well as immune suppression with poorer resistance to infection. Vitamin D status may influence the bacterial flora that constitute the microbiome and affect immune function through this route.
summary:
The paper "Vitamin D and Immunity" by Lucas et al. explores the relationship between vitamin D deficiency and immune function, particularly its implications for autoimmune diseases and infections. The main objective is to understand how vitamin D influences immune responses and the potential mechanisms involved.

The authors review epidemiological studies that suggest a correlation between low vitamin D levels and increased incidence of autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes. They discuss various methods, including observational studies and mechanistic research, to investigate how vitamin D affects immune cell function and the microbiome.

Key findings indicate that vitamin D plays a crucial role in modulating immune responses, with evidence supporting its involvement in both enhancing innate immunity and suppressing adaptive immunity. However, despite these associations, clinical trials of vitamin D supplementation have often yielded null results regarding its effectiveness in preventing or treating immune-related diseases. The authors highlight the complexity of vitamin D's role, noting that its effects may be influenced by factors such as the timing of supplementation, genetic variability, and the potential for vitamin D-independent pathways related to sun exposure.

In conclusion, while vitamin D deficiency is linked to various immune disorders, the evidence for supplementation as a preventive or therapeutic measure remains inconclusive. The authors suggest that future research should focus on understanding the timing and context of vitamin D interventions, as well as the interplay between vitamin D, the microbiome, and immune regulation. This could have significant implications for public health strategies aimed at improving vitamin D status in populations at risk for autoimmune diseases.

title: Macronutrient metabolism by the human gut microbiome: major fermentation by-products and their impact on host health
abstract: The human gut microbiome is a critical component of digestion, breaking down complex carbohydrates, proteins, and to a lesser extent fats that reach the lower gastrointestinal tract. This process results in a multitude of microbial metabolites that can act both locally and systemically (after being absorbed into the bloodstream). The impact of these biochemicals on human health is complex, as both potentially beneficial and potentially toxic metabolites can be yielded from such microbial pathways, and in some cases, these effects are dependent upon the metabolite concentration or organ locality. The aim of this review is to summarize our current knowledge of how macronutrient metabolism by the gut microbiome influences human health.
summary:
The main objective of the review by Oliphant and Allen-Vercoe is to summarize the influence of macronutrient metabolism by the human gut microbiome on human health, focusing on the fermentation by-products generated from carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. The authors employ a comprehensive literature review to discuss various microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), alcohols, ammonia, and other compounds derived from the fermentation of dietary macronutrients.

Key findings indicate that the gut microbiome plays a crucial role in metabolizing complex dietary components, producing metabolites that can have both beneficial and harmful effects on host health. SCFAs, particularly butyrate, are highlighted for their positive impact on intestinal health, including promoting epithelial integrity and exerting anti-inflammatory effects. Conversely, the metabolism of proteins can yield toxic by-products, such as ammonia and hydrogen sulfide, which may harm the host if produced in excess.

The review concludes that understanding the intricate relationship between gut microbiome metabolism and host health is essential for developing dietary strategies aimed at enhancing well-being. The authors emphasize the need for further research to fill knowledge gaps regarding specific microbial taxa and their metabolic pathways, which could lead to improved health outcomes and better management of gastrointestinal diseases. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of a balanced diet in supporting a healthy gut microbiome and, consequently, overall health.

title: Omega-3 fatty acids for breast cancer prevention and survivorship
abstract: Women with evidence of high intake ratios of the marine omega-3 fatty acids eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) relative to the omega-6 arachidonic acid have been found to have a reduced risk of breast cancer compared with those with low ratios in some but not all case–control and cohort studies. If increasing EPA and DHA relative to arachidonic acid is effective in reducing breast cancer risk, likely mechanisms include reduction in proinflammatory lipid derivatives, inhibition of nuclear factor-κB-induced cytokine production, and decreased growth factor receptor signaling as a result of alteration in membrane lipid rafts. Primary prevention trials with either risk biomarkers or cancer incidence as endpoints are underway but final results of these trials are currently unavailable. EPA and DHA supplementation is also being explored in an effort to help prevent or alleviate common problems after a breast cancer diagnosis, including cardiac and cognitive dysfunction and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
summary:
The paper titled "Omega-3 fatty acids for breast cancer prevention and survivorship" by Fabian et al. explores the potential role of marine omega-3 fatty acids, specifically eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), in reducing breast cancer risk and improving outcomes for survivors. The main objective is to assess whether increasing the ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acids can lower breast cancer incidence and enhance survivorship.

The authors review various studies, including case-control and cohort studies, which indicate that higher intake ratios of EPA and DHA relative to arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid) are associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer. They discuss the mechanisms through which omega-3 fatty acids may exert protective effects, such as reducing pro-inflammatory lipid derivatives and inhibiting pathways that promote cancer cell growth.

Key findings suggest that while some studies show a significant reduction in breast cancer risk with increased omega-3 intake, results are inconsistent across different populations and methodologies. Notably, a meta-analysis indicates that each 0.1 increase in the dietary omega-3 to omega-6 ratio correlates with a 6% reduction in breast cancer risk.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the need for further research, particularly large-scale clinical trials, to establish definitive recommendations for omega-3 supplementation in breast cancer prevention and survivorship. The implications of this research could lead to dietary guidelines that incorporate omega-3 fatty acids as a strategic measure for reducing breast cancer risk and improving health outcomes for survivors.

title: Gut microbiome development along the colorectal adenoma–carcinoma sequence
abstract: Colorectal cancer, a commonly diagnosed cancer in the elderly, often develops slowly from benign polyps called adenoma. The gut microbiota is believed to be directly involved in colorectal carcinogenesis. The identity and functional capacity of the adenoma- or carcinoma- related gut microbe(s), however, have not been surveyed in a comprehensive manner. Here we perform a metagenome-wide association study (MGWAS) on stools from advanced adenoma and carcinoma patients and from healthy subjects, revealing microbial genes, strains and functions enriched in each group. An analysis of potential risk factors indicates that high intake of red meat relative to fruits and vegetables appears to associate with outgrowth of bacteria that might contribute to a more hostile gut environment. These findings suggest that faecal microbiome-based strategies may be useful for early diagnosis and treatment of colorectal adenoma or carcinoma.
summary:
The main objective of the study was to investigate the gut microbiome's role in the progression from colorectal adenoma to carcinoma, identifying specific microbial genes and functions associated with these conditions. The researchers conducted a metagenome-wide association study (MGWAS) on stool samples from 156 individuals, including patients with advanced adenomas, colorectal carcinoma, and healthy controls. 

Key findings revealed significant differences in microbial gene richness and composition among the groups. Notably, the gut microbiome of carcinoma patients exhibited an increase in pathogenic bacteria such as Bacteroides and Fusobacterium, while beneficial bacteria like Bifidobacterium were diminished. The study also highlighted dietary influences, showing that a high intake of red meat correlated with the presence of harmful bacteria, whereas fruit and vegetable consumption was associated with healthier microbiome profiles.

The study concluded that the gut microbiome undergoes profound shifts during the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, suggesting that specific microbial markers could serve as potential diagnostic tools for early detection of colorectal cancer. The findings imply that microbiome-based interventions, alongside dietary modifications, could be promising strategies for colorectal cancer prevention and management.

title: Dietary fiber metabolites regulate innate lymphoid cell responses
abstract: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) rapidly undergo expansion in population size and functional maturation in response to cytokines that signal infection, tissue damage, or changes in physiology. Optimal ILC responses are shaped, in part, by the microbiota but the mechanisms remain unclear. We report that short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), produced by the commensal microbiota from dietary fibers, support optimal expansion of ILCs, including ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3 in the intestines through their G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). While this function is primarily important for intestinal ILC populations, it can also boost ILC responses in other tissues depending on host condition. ILCs express multiple GPCRs that detect SCFAs. Interestingly, we found that the expression of SCFA receptors, such as Ffar2 and Ffar3, by ILCs is induced by SCFAs. GPCR triggering by SCFAs co-stimulates the activation of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), Stat3, Stat5, and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), which is important for ILC proliferation. While Ffar2 signaling promotes ILC2 proliferation, SCFAs can suppress ILC2 proliferation through a non-Ffar2-mediated mechanism. In conclusion, our findings indicate that SCFAs, as the major mediator of healthy microbiota and nutritional status, function to maintain optimal numbers of ILCs in peripheral tissues during infection and inflammatory responses.
summary:
The main objective of the study by Sepahi et al. was to investigate how short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), produced by the commensal microbiota from dietary fibers, regulate the responses of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) in the intestines and other tissues. The researchers employed various methods, including dietary interventions in mouse models, flow cytometry, and gene expression analysis, to assess the impact of SCFAs on ILC populations and their functional maturation.

Key findings revealed that SCFAs enhance the expansion of ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3 populations through their interaction with G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) such as Ffar2 and Ffar3. The study demonstrated that SCFAs not only promote ILC proliferation but also induce the expression of their own receptors on ILCs. Notably, while Ffar2 signaling was crucial for ILC expansion during infection, SCFAs exhibited a dual role, positively regulating ILC3 but negatively affecting ILC2 proliferation.

In conclusion, the findings indicate that SCFAs play a vital role in maintaining optimal ILC populations during immune responses, particularly in the intestines. The study highlights the importance of dietary fibers and their metabolites in shaping immune responses, suggesting potential therapeutic implications for enhancing immunity through dietary interventions in conditions characterized by dysregulated ILC activity.

title: Influence of diet on the gut microbiome and implications for human health
abstract: Recent studies have suggested that the intestinal microbiome plays an important role in modulating risk of several chronic diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. At the same time, it is now understood that diet plays a significant role in shaping the microbiome, with experiments showing that dietary alterations can induce large, temporary microbial shifts within 24 h. Given this association, there may be significant therapeutic utility in altering microbial composition through diet. This review systematically evaluates current data regarding the effects of several common dietary components on intestinal microbiota. We show that consumption of particular types of food produces predictable shifts in existing host bacterial genera. Furthermore, the identity of these bacteria affects host immune and metabolic parameters, with broad implications for human health.
summary:
The main objective of the review by Singh et al. (2017) is to evaluate the influence of diet on the gut microbiome and its implications for human health, particularly concerning chronic diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

The authors conducted a systematic literature review, analyzing studies from the MEDLINE database that explored the relationship between various dietary components and gut microbiota composition. They included human and animal studies, focusing on randomized controlled trials, cross-sectional studies, and case-control studies published between 1970 and 2015.

Key findings indicate that dietary changes can rapidly alter gut microbiota composition within 24 hours, with specific foods leading to predictable shifts in bacterial genera. For instance, high-protein diets tend to increase certain bacteria associated with inflammation, while high-fiber diets promote beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which have anti-inflammatory effects. The review also highlights that different diets, such as Western, vegetarian, and Mediterranean, have distinct impacts on gut microbiota diversity and health outcomes.

The authors conclude that understanding the relationship between diet and the gut microbiome can inform therapeutic strategies for managing chronic diseases. They emphasize the potential for dietary interventions to modify microbial composition, thereby improving health outcomes and providing valuable insights for both practitioners and patients. This knowledge underscores the importance of dietary choices in shaping the gastrointestinal ecosystem and overall health.

title: Long chain omega-3 fatty acids and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains the commonest health problem in developed countries, and residual risk after implementing all current therapies is still high. The use of marine omega-3 fatty acids (DHA and EPA) has been recommended to reduce cardiovascular risk by multiple mechanisms. This systematic review aims to update the current evidence on the influence of omega-3 on the rate of cardiovascular events.
summary:
The paper titled "Long chain omega-3 fatty acids and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review" aims to evaluate the impact of marine omega-3 fatty acids (DHA and EPA) on cardiovascular events. The authors conducted a systematic review of clinical trials and randomized controlled trials, focusing on studies with a minimum duration of six months, comparing omega-3 intake (via capsules or diet) against placebo or usual diet.

The review included 21 out of 452 initially identified studies, which collectively involved over 50,000 participants. The primary outcome measured was the incidence of cardiovascular events, while secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiac death, and coronary events. Statistical analyses were performed using the Mantel-Haenszel method, assessing heterogeneity among studies.

Key findings revealed a 10% overall reduction in the risk of cardiovascular events (odds ratio [OR] 0.90), a 9% decrease in cardiac death (OR 0.91), and an 18% reduction in coronary events (OR 0.82). Although there was a trend towards lower total mortality (5% reduction, OR 0.95), this did not reach statistical significance.

The authors conclude that marine omega-3 fatty acids are effective in reducing cardiovascular events, particularly in high-risk populations. They emphasize the need for increased omega-3 consumption in Western diets, as current intake levels are below recommended amounts. The findings support the American Heart Association's recommendations for omega-3 intake, highlighting its potential role in cardiovascular disease prevention. The study underscores the importance of further research to explore the mechanisms behind omega-3's protective effects and to refine dietary guidelines.

title: Interaction between drugs and the gut microbiome
abstract: The human gut microbiome is a complex ecosystem that can mediate the interaction of the human host with their environment. The interaction between gut microbes and commonly used non-antibiotic drugs is complex and bidirectional: gut microbiome composition can be influenced by drugs, but, vice versa, the gut microbiome can also influence an individual’s response to a drug by enzymatically transforming the drug’s structure and altering its bioavailability, bioactivity or toxicity (pharmacomicrobiomics). The gut microbiome can also indirectly impact an individual’s response to immunotherapy in cancer treatment. In this review we discuss the bidirectional interactions between microbes and drugs, describe the changes in gut microbiota induced by commonly used non-antibiotic drugs, and their potential clinical consequences and summarise how the microbiome impacts drug effectiveness and its role in immunotherapy. Understanding how the microbiome metabolises drugs and reduces treatment efficacy will unlock the possibility of modulating the gut microbiome to improve treatment.
summary:
The main objective of the paper by Weersma et al. (2020) is to explore the complex bidirectional interactions between commonly used non-antibiotic drugs and the gut microbiome, focusing on how these interactions can influence drug efficacy and safety.

The authors employed a review methodology, synthesizing findings from various studies, including human cohort studies and animal experiments, to analyze how drugs like proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), metformin, and others affect gut microbiome composition and function. They also examined how the microbiome can modulate drug metabolism and therapeutic responses.

Key findings indicate that many non-antibiotic drugs significantly alter gut microbiome diversity and composition. For instance, PPIs were associated with decreased microbial diversity and increased susceptibility to infections like Clostridium difficile. Metformin was shown to modify the microbiome in ways that may enhance its glucose-lowering effects. Furthermore, the gut microbiome can enzymatically transform drugs, impacting their bioavailability and toxicity.

The conclusions emphasize the importance of understanding these interactions to optimize drug therapies and mitigate adverse effects. The paper suggests that insights into pharmacomicrobiomics could lead to strategies for modulating the gut microbiome to improve treatment outcomes, particularly in chronic conditions and during cancer immunotherapy. This highlights the need for a reevaluation of the widespread use of certain medications, particularly PPIs, considering their potential long-term effects on gut health and overall patient outcomes.

title: Long-chain omega-3 fatty acids and the brain: a review of the independent and shared effects of EPA, DPA and DHA
abstract: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) exhibit neuroprotective properties and represent a potential treatment for a variety of neurodegenerative and neurological disorders. However, traditionally there has been a lack of discrimination between the different omega-3 PUFAs and effects have been broadly accredited to the series as a whole. Evidence for unique effects of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and more recently docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) is growing. The purpose of this review is to highlight how a detailed understanding of these effects is essential to improving understanding of their therapeutic potential.
summary:
The main objective of this review by Simon C. Dyall is to explore the distinct and shared effects of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids—eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and docosapentaenoic acid (DPA)—on brain health, particularly in the context of aging and neurodegenerative disorders.

The review employs a comprehensive literature analysis, focusing on the biochemistry and metabolism of these omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) in the central nervous system (CNS). It examines their neuroprotective properties, anti-inflammatory effects, and roles in neuronal membrane composition and function.

Key findings indicate that while DHA is the most abundant omega-3 fatty acid in the brain and plays a crucial role in neuronal membranes, EPA and DPA also exhibit unique effects. For instance, EPA has been linked to improvements in mood disorders, while DHA is more commonly associated with neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's disease. DPA, previously less studied, is gaining recognition for its potential neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory roles.

The conclusions drawn from this review emphasize the necessity of distinguishing between the effects of EPA, DPA, and DHA in clinical research and dietary recommendations. Understanding their individual contributions could lead to more targeted therapeutic interventions for neurological conditions and improved dietary guidelines to enhance brain health. This nuanced perspective on omega-3 PUFAs may ultimately refine approaches to treating neurodegenerative diseases and promote healthier aging.

title: Vitamin D in Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection: Influence on Immunity and Disease
abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection typically have hypovitaminosis D, which is linked to a large number of pathologies, including immune disorders and infectious diseases. Vitamin D (VitD) is a key regulator of host defense against infections by activating genes and pathways that enhance innate and adaptive immunity. VitD mediates its biological effects by binding to the Vitamin D receptor (VDR), and activating and regulating multiple cellular pathways. Single nucleotide polymorphisms in genes from those pathways have been associated with protection from HIV-1 infection. High levels of VitD and VDR expression are also associated with natural resistance to HIV-1 infection. Conversely, VitD deficiency is linked to more inflammation and immune activation, low peripheral blood CD4+ T-cells, faster progression of HIV disease, and shorter survival time in HIV-infected patients. VitD supplementation and restoration to normal values in HIV-infected patients may improve immunologic recovery during combination antiretroviral therapy, reduce levels of inflammation and immune activation, and increase immunity against pathogens. Additionally, VitD may protect against the development of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome events, pulmonary tuberculosis, and mortality among HIV-infected patients. In summary, this review suggests that VitD deficiency may contribute to the pathogenesis of HIV infection. Also, VitD supplementation seems to reverse some alterations of the immune system, supporting the use of VitD supplementation as prophylaxis, especially in individuals with more severe VitD deficiency.
summary:
The main objective of the paper "Vitamin D in Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection: Influence on Immunity and Disease" is to explore the role of vitamin D (VitD) in the context of HIV infection, particularly its effects on immune function and disease progression.

The authors conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature to analyze the relationship between VitD levels and HIV infection outcomes. They examined mechanisms by which VitD influences immune responses, including its role in regulating inflammation, innate and adaptive immunity, and the expression of the vitamin D receptor (VDR).

Key findings indicate that a significant proportion (70-85%) of individuals living with HIV experience VitD deficiency, which is associated with increased inflammation, lower CD4+ T-cell counts, and faster disease progression. Conversely, adequate VitD levels are linked to improved immune responses, reduced inflammation, and potentially better survival rates. VitD supplementation may enhance immunologic recovery during antiretroviral therapy and decrease the risk of opportunistic infections and complications such as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

In conclusion, the review suggests that VitD deficiency may contribute to the pathogenesis of HIV infection by impairing immune responses. The authors advocate for VitD supplementation as a potential adjunct therapy for HIV-infected individuals, particularly those with severe deficiency, to improve immune function and health outcomes. Further research is needed to establish standardized guidelines for VitD supplementation in this population.

filename: Beneficial Outcomes of Omega-6 and Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids on Human .pdf
title: Beneficial Outcomes of Omega-6 and Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids on Human Health: An Update for 2021
abstract: Oxidative stress and inflammation have been recognized as important contributors to the risk of chronic non-communicable diseases. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) may regulate the antioxidant signaling pathway and modulate inflammatory processes. They also influence hepatic lipid metabolism and physiological responses of other organs, including the heart. Longitudinal prospective cohort studies demonstrate that there is an association between moderate intake of the omega-6 PUFA linoleic acid and lower risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), most likely as a result of lower blood cholesterol concentration. Current evidence suggests that increasing intake of arachidonic acid (up to 1500 mg/day) has no adverse effect on platelet aggregation and blood clotting, immune function and markers of inflammation, but may benefit muscle and cognitive performance. Many studies show that higher intakes of omega-3 PUFAs, especially eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), are associated with a lower incidence of chronic diseases characterized by elevated inflammation, including CVDs. This is because of the multiple molecular and cellular actions of EPA and DHA. Intervention trials using EPA + DHA indicate benefit on CVD mortality and a significant inverse linear dose–response relationship has been found between EPA + DHA intake and CVD outcomes. In addition to their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory roles, omega-3 fatty acids are considered to regulate platelet homeostasis and lower risk of thrombosis, which together indicate their potential use in COVID-19 therapy.
summary:
The paper by Djuricic and Calder aims to update the understanding of the health benefits associated with omega-6 and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly in relation to chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and inflammation. 

The authors conducted a review of existing literature, including longitudinal cohort studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs), to analyze the effects of omega-6 (e.g., linoleic acid) and omega-3 (e.g., eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid) fatty acids on human health.

Key findings indicate that moderate intake of omega-6 fatty acids is linked to a reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) through mechanisms such as lowering blood cholesterol levels. Additionally, higher omega-3 intake is associated with lower incidence rates of chronic diseases characterized by inflammation. The review highlights that omega-3 PUFAs may have protective roles against CVD mortality and could potentially be beneficial in managing conditions like COVID-19 due to their anti-inflammatory properties.

The authors conclude that both omega-6 and omega-3 PUFAs play significant roles in regulating inflammation and oxidative stress, which are critical factors in the development of NCDs. They suggest that dietary adjustments to increase omega-6 and omega-3 intake could have substantial public health implications, particularly in reducing the burden of chronic diseases. The paper emphasizes the need for further research to clarify the effects of specific fatty acids on health outcomes and to optimize dietary recommendations.

title: SCFA: mechanisms and functional importance in the gut
abstract: In recent years, the importance of the gut microbiota in human health has been revealed and many publications have highlighted its role as a key component of human physiology. Owing to the use of modern sequencing approaches, the characterisation of the microbiome in healthy individuals and in disease has demonstrated a disturbance of the microbiota, or dysbiosis, associated with pathological conditions. The microbiota establishes a symbiotic cross-talk with their host: commensal microbes benefit from the nutrient-rich environment provided by the gut and the microbiota produces hundreds of proteins and metabolites that modulate key functions of the host, including nutrient processing, maintenance of energy homoeostasis and immune system development. Many bacteria-derived metabolites originate from dietary sources. Among them, an important role has been attributed to the metabolites derived from the bacterial fermentation of dietary fibres, namely SCFA linking host nutrition to intestinal homoeostasis maintenance.
summary:
The main objective of the paper is to explore the mechanisms and functional importance of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by gut microbiota in relation to gut health and host immunity. The authors review recent findings on SCFAs, particularly butyrate, and their roles in modulating intestinal functions, metabolism, and immune responses.

The methods employed include a comprehensive literature review of studies utilizing modern sequencing techniques to characterize the gut microbiome and its metabolites, alongside experimental data from in vitro and in vivo models examining SCFA production, transport, and their physiological effects.

Key findings indicate that SCFAs, especially butyrate, serve as crucial energy sources for intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and influence various cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, and immune modulation. SCFAs regulate gut barrier integrity, enhance mucus production, and promote the secretion of gut hormones, which are vital for metabolic homeostasis. Additionally, dysbiosis, characterized by reduced SCFA-producing bacteria, is linked to several pathological conditions, including metabolic disorders and inflammatory diseases.

In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the significant role of SCFAs in maintaining gut health and their potential therapeutic implications. By understanding SCFA mechanisms, researchers can explore dietary interventions and microbiota modulation as strategies to improve health outcomes and manage diseases associated with gut dysbiosis. The findings highlight the intricate relationship between diet, gut microbiota, and host physiology, underscoring the importance of SCFAs in promoting overall well-being.

title: Dietary Omega-3 Fatty Acid Deficiency and Visual Loss in Infant Rhesus Monkeys
abstract: Linolenic acid (18:3w3) is a dietary precursor of docosahexaenoic acid (22:6w3), the major fatty acid in the photoreceptor membranes of the retina. We hypothesized that rhesus monkeys deprived of dietary w-3 fatty acids during prenatal and postnatal development would show plasma depletion of these fatty acids and visual impairment. Semipurified diets low in w-3 fatty acids were fed to one group of adult female rhesus monkeys throughout pregnancy and to their infants from birth. A control group of mothers and infants received similar diets but supplying ample linolenic acid. In the plasma phospholipids of deficient infants, linolenic acid was generally undetectable and 22:6w3 levels became progressively depleted, falling from 42% of control values at birth to 21% at 4 wk, 9% at 8 wk, and 6% at 12 wk of age. The visual acuity of the deprived infants, as measured by the preferential looking method, was reduced by one-fourth at 4 wk (P < 0.05) and by one-half at 8 and 12 wk (P < 0.0005) compared with control infants. These results suggest that w-3 fatty acids may be an essential nutrient, and that 22:6w3 may have a specific function in the photoreceptor membranes of the retina.
summary:
The main objective of the study by Neuringer et al. was to investigate the effects of dietary omega-3 fatty acid deficiency on visual development in infant rhesus monkeys. The researchers hypothesized that deprivation of omega-3 fatty acids during prenatal and postnatal development would lead to decreased plasma levels of these fatty acids and subsequent visual impairment.

To test this hypothesis, adult female rhesus monkeys were fed a semipurified diet low in omega-3 fatty acids (safflower oil) throughout pregnancy and their infants continued on the same diet from birth. A control group received a diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids (soybean oil). Plasma lipid fatty acid composition was analyzed, and visual acuity was assessed using a preferential looking method at various ages.

Key findings revealed that infants deprived of omega-3 fatty acids exhibited a significant depletion of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6w3) in plasma phospholipids, with levels dropping to undetectable amounts by 12 weeks. Visual acuity was significantly impaired in the deficient group, with thresholds reduced by approximately 50% compared to controls by 8 and 12 weeks of age.

The study concluded that omega-3 fatty acids, particularly DHA, are essential for normal visual development in primates. The findings suggest that dietary omega-3 fatty acid content is crucial for infants, indicating potential implications for infant nutrition, particularly in the formulation of infant formulas that may lack adequate levels of these essential fatty acids.

title: Impact of vitamin D on immune function: lessons learned from genome-wide analysis
abstract: Immunomodulatory responses to the active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, 1,25D) have been recognized for many years, but it is only in the last 5 years that the potential role of this in normal human immune function has been recognized. Genome-wide analyses have played a pivotal role in redefining our perspective on vitamin D and immunity. The description of increased vitamin D receptor (VDR) and 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) expression in macrophages following a pathogen challenge, has underlined the importance of intracrine vitamin D as key mediator of innate immune function. It is now clear that both macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) are able to respond to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25D), the major circulating vitamin D metabolite, thereby providing a link between the function of these cells and the variations in vitamin D status common to many humans.
summary:
The main objective of the review article by Chun et al. (2014) is to explore the impact of vitamin D, particularly its active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), on immune function, emphasizing insights gained from genome-wide analyses. The authors discuss how these analyses have reshaped our understanding of vitamin D's role in both innate and adaptive immunity.

The methods employed include genome-wide analyses, DNA array studies, and in vitro experiments that investigate the expression of vitamin D receptors (VDR) and the enzyme responsible for converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form (CYP27B1) in immune cells like macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs). These methods reveal how vitamin D influences immune responses, particularly in relation to pathogen challenges.

Key findings indicate that vitamin D enhances the expression of antibacterial proteins, modulates antigen presentation, and promotes immune tolerance while suppressing inflammation. Specifically, it was found that macrophages and DCs can respond to circulating vitamin D, which influences their function and the overall immune response. The review also highlights the role of vitamin D in regulating cytokine signaling pathways, which can either enhance or inhibit immune responses.

In conclusion, the authors emphasize that vitamin D plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy immune system, with implications for understanding immune-related diseases and the potential need for vitamin D supplementation in individuals with varying vitamin D status. The findings suggest that optimizing vitamin D levels could be beneficial for enhancing immune function and preventing disease, particularly in populations at risk of deficiency.

title: Temporal development of the gut microbiome in early childhood from the TEDDY study
abstract: The development of the microbiome from infancy to childhood is dependent on a range of factors, with microbial–immune crosstalk during this time thought to be involved in the pathobiology of later life diseases such as persistent islet autoimmunity and type 1 diabetes. However, to our knowledge, no studies have performed extensive characterization of the microbiome in early life in a large, multi-centre population. Here we analyse longitudinal stool samples from 903 children between 3 and 46 months of age by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic sequencing, as part of the TEDDY study. We show that the developing gut microbiome undergoes three distinct phases of microbiome progression: a developmental phase (months 3–14), a transitional phase (months 15–30), and a stable phase (months 31–46).
summary:
The main objective of this study was to characterize the longitudinal development of the gut microbiome in early childhood, particularly in relation to factors influencing microbiome composition and potential associations with islet autoimmunity (IA) and type 1 diabetes (T1D). The research utilized longitudinal stool samples from 903 children aged 3 to 46 months, collected as part of the TEDDY study, employing 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic sequencing.

Key findings revealed that the gut microbiome undergoes three distinct phases: a developmental phase (3-14 months), a transitional phase (15-30 months), and a stable phase (31-46 months). Breastfeeding emerged as the most significant factor influencing microbiome structure, with higher levels of Bifidobacterium species observed in breastfed infants. The cessation of breastfeeding was linked to faster microbiome maturation, characterized by increased Firmicutes levels. Additionally, birth mode and environmental factors, such as geographical location and household exposures, were found to impact microbiome development.

The study concluded that the first year of life is critical for microbiome development, primarily driven by breastfeeding, while subsequent phases reflect a transition to a more stable microbiome. Although subtle associations were noted between microbiome composition and the development of IA or T1D, the overall microbiome dynamics did not show strong correlations with disease onset. These findings provide a foundation for further investigations into microbial-immune interactions and their implications for long-term health, particularly in populations at risk for autoimmune conditions.

title: The importance of nutrition in pregnancy and lactation: lifelong consequences
authors: Hora Soltani, PhD, MMedSci, RM, PGDip, PGCert
abstract: Most women in the United States do not meet the recommendations for healthful nutrition and weight before and during pregnancy. Women and providers often ask what a healthy diet for a pregnant woman should look like. The message should be “eat better, not more.” This can be achieved by basing diet on a variety of nutrient-dense, whole foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats with omega-3 fatty acids that include nuts and seeds, and fish, in place of poorer quality highly processed foods. Such a diet embodies nutritional density and is less likely to be accompanied by excessive energy intake than the standard American diet consisting of increased intakes of processed foods, fatty red meat, and sweetened foods and beverages. Women who report “prudent” or “health-conscious” eating patterns before and/or during pregnancy may have fewer pregnancy complications and adverse child health outcomes.
summary:
The paper titled "The importance of nutrition in pregnancy and lactation: lifelong consequences" aims to highlight the critical role of maternal nutrition before, during, and after pregnancy in influencing both maternal and offspring health outcomes. The authors emphasize that many women in the U.S. do not meet nutritional guidelines, which can lead to adverse pregnancy outcomes.

The researchers conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature, drawing on observational studies and systematic reviews to assess the impact of dietary patterns on pregnancy complications and child health. They focused on the importance of nutrient-dense diets rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats, while cautioning against fad diets that restrict macronutrients.

Key findings indicate that women who maintain a "prudent" dietary pattern experience fewer complications, such as gestational diabetes and low birth weight in infants. Additionally, maternal prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) significantly influences pregnancy outcomes, with both underweight and obesity linked to risks for the mother and child. The study also highlights the importance of early nutritional interventions, suggesting that improvements in maternal health can lead to better fetal growth and long-term health for both mothers and children.

In conclusion, the authors advocate for enhanced nutritional counseling and support for women of reproductive age, emphasizing that optimal nutrition can lead to favorable pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of chronic diseases in offspring. They call for further research to fill existing knowledge gaps and encourage healthcare providers to prioritize maternal nutrition in clinical practice.

title: Dietary Protein and Muscle Mass: Translating Science to Application and Health Benefit
abstract: Adequate consumption of dietary protein is critical for the maintenance of optimal health during normal growth and aging. The current Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein is defined as the minimum amount required to prevent lean body mass loss, but is often misrepresented and misinterpreted as a recommended optimal intake. Over the past two decades, the potential muscle-related benefits achieved by consuming higher-protein diets have become increasingly clear. Despite greater awareness of how higher-protein diets might be advantageous for muscle mass, actual dietary patterns, particularly as they pertain to protein, have remained relatively unchanged in American adults. This lack of change may, in part, result from confusion over the purported detrimental effects of higher-protein diets. title: Amino acid balance across tissues of the forearm in postabsorptive man. Effects of insulin at two dose levels
abstract: Amino acid balance across skeletal muscle and across subcutaneous adipose tissue plus skin of the forearm has been quantified in postabsorptive man before and after insulin infusion into the brachial artery. Skeletal muscle released significant amounts of alpha amino nitrogen after an overnight fast. Most individual amino acids were released. Alanine output was by far the greatest. The pattern of release probably reflects both the composition of muscle protein undergoing degradation and de novo synthesis of alanine by transamination. A significant correlation was observed between the extent of release of each amino acid and its ambient arterial concentration. Elevation of forearm insulin in eight subjects from postabsorptive (12 muU/ml) to high physiologic levels (157 muU/ml) in addition to stimulating muscle glucose uptake blocked muscle alpha amino nitrogen release by 74%. Statin-associated muscle symptoms: impact on statin therapy—European Atherosclerosis Society Consensus Panel Statement on Assessment, Aetiology and Management
abstract: Statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS) are one of the principal reasons for statin non-adherence and/or discontinuation, contributing to adverse cardiovascular outcomes. This European Atherosclerosis Society (EAS) Consensus Panel overviews current understanding of the pathophysiology of statin-associated myopathy, and provides guidance for diagnosis and management of SAMS. Statin-associated myopathy, with significant elevation of serum creatine kinase (CK), is a rare but serious side effect of statins, affecting 1 per 1000 to 1 per 10 000 people on standard statin doses. Statin-associated muscle symptoms cover a broader range of clinical presentations, usually with normal or minimally elevated CK levels, with a prevalence of 7-29% in registries and observational studies. Preclinical studies show that statins decrease mitochondrial function, attenuate energy production, and alter muscle protein degradation, thereby providing a potential link between statins and muscle symptoms; controlled mechanistic and genetic studies in humans are necessary to further understanding. The Panel proposes to identify SAMS by symptoms typical of statin myalgia (i.e. muscle pain or aching) and their temporal association with discontinuation and response to repetitive statin re-challenge. In people with SAMS, the Panel recommends the use of a maximally tolerated statin dose combined with non-statin lipid-lowering therapies to attain recommended low-density lipoprotein cholesterol targets.
